implication: (inference) P&W's aftermarket halved for three quarters in COVID and took until 2021-22 to rebound; aftermarket revenue is flight-hour-driven and highly cyclical in the short term.

finding: The GTF installed base in the GS model (cumulative deliveries) grew from 124 engines in 2016 to 439 in 2017, 1005 in 2018, 1743.5 in 2019, 2239.5 in 2020, 3574.5 in 2022, 4474.5 in 2023 and 5482.5 in 2024.

During the GTF ramp P&W commercial OE sales changed y/y by -3% in 1Q18, 20% in 2Q18, 74% in 4Q18 and 35% in 1Q19, then -7% in 4Q19, while commercial aftermarket growth slowed from 18% in 1Q18 to 1% in 1Q19 and 0% in 4Q19.
P&W military engine shipments rose from 31 in 1Q16 and 41 in 4Q17 to 47 in 4Q18, 65 in 4Q19 and 72 in 2Q20, then eased to 55 in 4Q21, 48 in 4Q22 and 42 in 1Q23.
GS's P&W one-time items include -$1,015mn in 4Q15 (-$1,052mn for 2015), -$194mn in 3Q17, -$300mn in 3Q18, -$990mn for 2020, -$3,143mn for 2023, -$266mn for 2024 and -$116mn in 2Q25.
implication: (inference) Large P&W charges recur roughly every few years (2015, 2020, 2023); a P&W agent should expect episodic $1-3bn hits, which RTX absorbs at group level.

finding: P&W large commercial engine shipments were 148, 149, 113, 128 in 1Q-4Q16 and 139, 139, 129, 130 in 1Q-4Q17 (totals 538 and 537).
GTF deliveries in the GS model went from 0 in 2014 to 124 in 2016, 315 in 2017, 566 in 2018 and 738.5 in 2019.
implication: (inference) P&W ramped a brand-new engine from zero to ~740 units a year in four years; the ramp itself was a choice to accept rising OE losses for installed-base share.

finding: P&W large commercial engine shipments were 124, 210, 198, 247 in 1Q-4Q18 and 189, 173, 165, 219 in 1Q-4Q19 (totals 779 and 746).
P&W's backlog rose from $71.1bn at end-2018 to $85.2bn at end-2019 (Collins $26.6bn to $29.5bn).
P&W large commercial engine shipments were 211, 92, 114, 129 in 1Q-4Q20 and 137, 144, 165, 177 in 1Q-4Q21 (totals 546 and 623).

P&W Canada engine deliveries in the GS model fell from 2,857 in 2014 and 2,532 in 2015 to 2,355 in 2019, 1,650 in 2020 and 1,965 in 2022, while military engine deliveries rose from 110 in 2014 to 215 in 2019 and 241 in 2020.
P&W large commercial engine shipments were 119, 177, 192, 224 in 1Q-4Q22 (total 712) and 167 in 1Q23, after which the tracker stops recording shipments.
P&W Canada engine shipments were 515 in 1Q16, 662 in 4Q16, 641 in 4Q18 and 631 in 4Q19, fell to 393 in 2Q20 and 379 in 3Q20, and were 542 in 4Q22 and 499 in 1Q23.

In 3Q23 P&W reported revenue of only $926mn (vs $5,701mn in 2Q23) and an operating loss of $2,482mn, after $2,895mn of one-time items (adjusted operating income $413mn); GS's P&W divested-revenue row holds -$5,401mn in 3Q23 and P&W organic growth for the quarter is shown as 17.6%.
implication: (inference) The size and form (a ~$5.4bn revenue adjustment alongside ~$2.9bn of one-time items in a single quarter) are consistent with the GTF powder-metal customer-compensation charge being booked mainly against revenue and taken up front in one quarter rather than spread over the fleet-inspection years.

finding: In 3Q23 P&W reported only $926m of sales (vs $5.70bn in 2Q23 and $6.44bn in 4Q23) and an operating loss of $2.48bn, leaving full-year 2023 at a $1.46bn loss.
implication: (inference) This is the GTF powder-metal charge: 3Q23 profit was about $2.8bn and sales about $5.1bn below the average of the neighbouring quarters, consistent with customer compensation booked as a reduction of sales. P&W took the cost up front in a single quarter.

finding: In 3Q23, when RTX booked a net loss of $933m, accounts payable and accrued liabilities added $3.57bn to operating cash flow, which was $3.32bn (FCF $2.75bn).
implication: (inference) The powder-metal charge was booked as an accrual, not paid in the quarter; the cash went out over 2024-26, consistent with compensating airlines over time.

finding: GTF deliveries in the GS model fell to 496 in 2020 (from 738.5 in 2019), then rose to 623 in 2021, 712 in 2022, 900 in 2023 and 1008 in 2024.
P&W segment sales were flat at about $7.4-7.7bn from 1997 to 2003 ($7.40bn 1997, $7.37bn 2000, $7.48bn 2003) while operating profit swung between $634m (1999) and $1.31bn (2001).
implication: (inference) Pre-2004 P&W was a mature, no-growth engine business earning roughly 8-17% margins, mostly from its installed base rather than new programmes.

finding: P&W sales grew from $8.28bn in 2004 to $13.85bn in 2008 (about 67%) and operating profit from $1.08bn to $2.12bn, a 15.3% margin in 2008.
implication: (inference) The 2004-08 cycle shows how profitable P&W is when it is harvesting a mature fleet without a new-engine launch: margins of 15-16% in 2005-08.

finding: P&W revenue was $7,402mn in 1997, $7,366mn in 2000 and $7,484mn in 2003, then grew to $9,295mn in 2005, $13,086mn in 2007 and $13,849mn in 2008 before falling 10.5% to $12,392mn in 2009.

implication: (inference) Before the GTF, with the V2500 and PW4000 installed bases maturing, P&W earned mid-teens margins and even expanded margin in the 2009 downturn.

finding: In the 2009 downturn P&W's organic revenue fell 8% and reported operating income fell from $2,122mn to $1,835mn after $190mn of one-time items, while adjusted operating income dipped only from $2,201mn to $2,025mn.
implication: (inference) In the 2009 recession P&W protected profit through restructuring (one-time charges) rather than letting margin fall.

finding: In the 2009 downturn P&W sales fell 10.5% to $12.39bn and operating profit 13.5% to $1.84bn (14.8% margin), recovering to $12.94bn and $1.99bn in 2010.
implication: (inference) The financial crisis cost P&W only about half a point of margin (15.3% to 14.8%), so a pure demand shock is far less damaging to it than a durability crisis or a new-programme ramp.

finding: From 2011 to 2014 P&W sales rose from $12.71bn to $14.51bn and operating profit ran $1.58-2.07bn, with a dip to $1.58bn (11.3% margin) in 2012 and a peak of $2.07bn (14.2%) in 2014.
implication: (inference) 2014 was the last year of 'old' P&W economics before GTF development and launch costs hit margins.

finding: P&W operating profit fell from $2.07bn in 2014 to $839m in 2015 (a 6.0% margin) on roughly flat sales of $14.08bn.
implication: (inference) The 2015 profit collapse at flat sales points to large one-off charges in the year before GTF entry into service; the model does not label them.

finding: P&W's adjusted operating margin slid from 16.4% in 2010 and 14.8% in 2011 to 12.0% in 2012, recovered to 14.7% in 2014, then fell through the GTF ramp to 13.4% (2015), 11.7% (2016), 9.3% (2017) and 8.8% (2018).
implication: (inference) P&W let segment margin fall by ~6 points (14.7% to 8.8%) over 2014-18 to fund GTF OE losses and ramp; margin was subordinated to winning the narrowbody installed base.

finding: During the GTF ramp P&W revenue grew from $14,894mn (2016) to $16,545mn (2017), $19,397mn (2018) and $20,902mn (2019), while adjusted operating income went $1,745mn, $1,546mn, $1,709mn and $1,934mn.
implication: (inference) Revenue rose 40% over 2016-19 while adjusted profit only returned to its 2016 level: growth from a new engine does not translate to profit until the aftermarket arrives.

finding: P&W's adjusted incremental operating margin was -18.0% in 2016, -12.0% in 2017, 5.7% in 2018 and 14.9% in 2019, with the adjusted margin at 9.3% in 2019.

During the 2016-2019 ramp P&W sales grew 40% from $14.89bn to $20.90bn, but operating profit stayed at $1.35-1.80bn, so the margin fell from 10.3% (2016) to 7.3% (2018) and only recovered to 8.6% in 2019.
implication: (inference) The new-engine ramp added revenue but not profit: OE engines shipped at negative margins diluted P&W from about 15% to about 7-9%. A next-generation engine launch should be expected to repeat this.

finding: In COVID, P&W quarterly sales fell from $5.35bn (1Q20) to $3.49bn (2Q20), it lost $457m and $615m in 2Q20 and 3Q20, and full-year 2020 was a $564m loss on $17.22bn sales.
implication: (inference) With a flying-hour-driven aftermarket, P&W's profit is highly geared to traffic: a 35% sales drop turned a $475m quarterly profit into losses.

finding: COVID cut P&W revenue from $20,902mn in 2019 to $17,224mn in 2020 (-17.6%), with quarterly revenue of $3,487mn in 2Q20 and $3,494mn in 3Q20 (organic -32.3% and -33.9%); 2021 revenue was $18,150mn.
P&W reported operating losses of $457mn in 2Q20 and $615mn in 3Q20 (adjusted losses of $151mn and $43mn); adjusted operating income was $426mn in 2020 and $487mn in 2021, margins of 2.5% and 2.7%.
implication: (inference) With GTF OE losses fixed and aftermarket collapsing, P&W's margin went to ~2.5% for two years; a P&W agent's downside in a demand shock is near-zero profit, not a modest dip.

finding: P&W recovered slowly after COVID: operating profit of $454m on $18.15bn sales in 2021 (2.5%) and $1.08bn on $20.53bn in 2022 (5.2%), with quarterly profit rising from $20m (1Q21) to $306m (4Q22).
implication: (inference) By 2022 P&W sales were back near 2019 levels but margins were about 3 points lower, as GTF OE deliveries grew faster than the aftermarket.

finding: P&W recovered to $20,530mn revenue and $1,250mn adjusted operating income in 2022 (6.1% margin, organic growth 13.3%), and $1,688mn adjusted operating income in 2023 (7.1% margin, organic growth 15.4%).

For 2023 P&W reported revenue of $18,296mn (-10.9% y/y) and an operating loss of $1,455mn (-8.0% margin), including $3,143mn of one-time items and a $5,401mn revenue adjustment in GS's divested-revenue row.
In 2024 P&W revenue was $28,066mn (53.4% reported, 18.4% organic), operating income $2,015mn after $266mn of one-time items, and adjusted operating income $2,281mn (8.1% margin, 6.1% incremental).
implication: (inference) Even with record revenue, P&W's incremental margin in 2024 was only ~6%: growth is still dominated by loss-making GTF OE and early aftermarket.

finding: P&W's share of group revenue (GS's recast RTX segment total) was 28.7% in 2012, 27.2% in 2019, 24.8% in 2020 and 33.7% in 2024, while its share of group adjusted operating income was 27.4%, 18.5%, 8.0% and 24.0%.
implication: (inference) P&W brings a third of RTX revenue but a smaller share of profit; its GTF losses are carried by a diversified parent (Collins, Raytheon), which is why P&W can price OE aggressively and survive multi-billion charges.

finding: In 2024 P&W sales rose every quarter from $6.46bn (1Q) to $7.57bn (4Q), reaching $28.07bn for the year with $2.02bn operating profit (7.2% margin).
implication: (inference) Even after the charge P&W earns only about 7% on sales; a new engine programme would start from a thin margin base.

finding: P&W reported revenue of $7,366mn, $7,631mn and $8,423mn in 1Q-3Q25, with adjusted operating income of $590mn, $608mn and $751mn; 3Q25 adjusted margin was 8.9% and organic growth 16.4%.
In the first three quarters of 2025 P&W sales were $7.37bn, $7.63bn and $8.42bn, with operating profit of $580m, $492m and $751m (about $23.4bn and $1.82bn year to date, a 7.8% margin).

GS records acquired revenue at P&W of $550mn a quarter from 3Q12 to 1Q13 and $375mn in 2Q13 ($1,100mn in 2012, $925mn in 2013), and P&W backlog rose from $22,400mn at end-2011 to $43,600mn at end-2012.
implication: (inference) The timing (from 3Q12, anniversaried after four quarters) matches P&W's mid-2012 purchase of Rolls-Royce's IAE/V2500 stake: P&W paid to consolidate the V2500 installed-base aftermarket rather than share it, a precedent for how it values narrowbody aftermarket control and how it has dealt with RR as a partner.

finding: Inside legacy UTC, P&W's share of operating income fell from 28.5% in 2007 ($2.01bn of $7.05bn) to 18.6% in 2019 ($1.67bn of $8.97bn), while its share of sales rose from 23.5% ($13.09bn of $55.72bn) to 27.1% ($20.89bn of $77.05bn).
implication: (inference) UTC funded the GTF from a diversified conglomerate (elevators, HVAC, aerospace systems); P&W's falling profit share during the ramp was carried by the other businesses.

finding: In 2024 P&W was the largest RTX segment by sales ($28.07bn of $80.81bn, 34.7%; Collins $28.28bn, Raytheon $26.78bn) but earned $2.02bn operating profit versus Collins $4.14bn and Raytheon $2.59bn.
implication: (inference) Within RTX, P&W is the lowest-margin segment and is funded alongside a defence business and Collins; group cash, not P&W's own profit, pays for a new engine.

doc: December 2015 Investor and Analyst Meeting (2016 Outlook)
speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: Airbus came out with this rate, 63, which is going to require us to add additional capital, really, not just at Paul's business but also at Dave's business.
finding: Pratt adds capacity capital in response to Airbus rate increases rather than capping its supply share.
trigger: Airbus raised A320-family production rate target to 63 per month
response: additional capex at Pratt and UTAS; capex not falling as fast as planned

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: There is going to be a relatively slow ramp in the first half of the year; no change to the full year, however. We still expect to deliver about 200 GTF engines. Most of those, of course, would go to Airbus... we're following the lead of Airbus on this
finding: Pratt follows Airbus's go-slow-then-fast entry-into-service plan while keeping its full-year target of about 200 GTFs.
trigger: Airbus signalled a 'go slow before you go fast' neo ramp
response: back-loaded 2016 GTF deliveries, kept the 200 full-year target

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: If oil goes from $30 a barrel, back to $90 a barrel, you'll have some reaction by the airlines in terms of what they're doing with the orders. If anything, I think it's opportunity for us if oil goes back up because we've got this very fuel-efficient engine.
finding: Pratt treats low fuel prices as reducing the urgency of new-engine aircraft and higher oil as a tailwind for GTF demand.
trigger: oil at about $30/bbl, Jet A about $1/gal
response: no change to strategy; sees upside if oil rises

speaker: Bob Leduc, President of Pratt & Whitney
quote: Of the 7,000 orders, about 3,000 are on the neo, about 1,300 engines each at Embraer and Bombardier, and the balance split between MRJ and Irkut... 58 customers will take delivery of Geared Turbofan powered airplanes. 17 of those new customers to Pratt, some of which are prior CFM56 customers that we switched
finding: The GTF order book is spread across five platforms, and some new customers were switched from CFM56.

doc: Company Conference Presentation (Deutsche Bank Industrials Summit, Jun 2016)
speaker: Akhil Johri, CFO
quote: Last time Pratt made 1,000 engines, large engines in a year was in 1980s, and we'll be getting back to that level of production in the next couple of years... having displaced GE on the Embraer platform with its Geared Turbofan and having displaced Rolls-Royce on the Gulfstream large business jet.
finding: Pratt took share from GE (Embraer E2) and Rolls-Royce (Gulfstream) and planned to return to 1980s-level large-engine output.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: they don't all go to Airbus... some go to Embraer, some go to Bombardier, some go to MRJ. There's also a large number of spares that we built in the first half of the year to support the in-service fleet... Airbus would like the engines sooner, but we're exactly on the production plan we committed to them
finding: Pratt split early GTF output across Airbus, other platforms and spare engines for the in-service fleet, defending its plan against Airbus's demand for more engines.
trigger: Airbus publicly wanted more GTF engines sooner
response: kept to committed production plan; prioritised spares for in-service fleet

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: one of our partners, IHI, will be coming online here in November with additional capacity. They'll start delivering fan blades at full rate production, we think, in January. We're also standing up a brand-new factory about 4 miles away from the current factory in Lansing, which will be mostly automated processes.
finding: Pratt dealt with the fan-blade bottleneck by adding a second source at partner IHI and building a new automated blade factory.
response: IHI second source; new automated Lansing factory (full rate April 2017)
lag: about 6-7 months from recognition to full-rate capacity

speaker: Akhil Johri, CFO
quote: our overall share on the Airbus 320neo is about 45% in terms of the engines that have been decided. But if you look at the last 12 months, that number is 56%.
finding: Despite the delivery problems, Pratt claimed about 45% of decided A320neo engine selections, rising to 56% over the previous 12 months.

response: over 50 spare engines in 2017
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: This year, we're going to build 350 to 400. A big -- a chunk of those, over 50 of those engines will be spares to give the support to the fleet going out there to make sure when we do have these issues that the customers are not impacted too much.
finding: P&W reserved more than 50 of its planned 2017 GTF output as spares to shield customers from durability problems.

response: selective, disciplined campaign bidding
speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: we are being very disciplined and selective with regard to the campaigns as well. I think if you look at -- and some of that shows up in our market share. We're not chasing market share here, but we are chasing a more profitable part of the engine portfolio
finding: P&W said it accepted lower market share by bidding selectively on engine campaigns, prioritising profitable deals over share.

response: additional spare engines to operators during upgrades
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: As we said before, neither of these are flight safety issues. And we'll continue to support operators with additional spare engines while we upgrade the fleet. The good news is, as I said, 13 operators, about 100 -- a little over 100 engines in service today, it's a manageable problem.
finding: P&W's standard crisis response was to supply extra spare engines to operators while upgrading the fleet; with about 100 engines at 13 operators it judged the problem manageable.

trigger: Gulfstream new business jet engine selection
response: won with PW800, displacing Rolls-Royce
speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: We also have replaced Rolls-Royce on the Gulfstream application, which starts to come into production next year.
finding: P&W displaced Rolls-Royce as engine supplier on a Gulfstream business jet application, showing it takes positions from RR where it can.

response: retained A320neo share vs CFM
speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: if you look at our market share on the 320neo, because that's the only place where there's competition on this, our market share since -- in the last 12 months, when a lot of these issues have been talked about, is exactly the same as the market share since the beginning of the program.
finding: P&W said its A320neo share against CFM's LEAP-1A held steady through the 2016-17 durability problems, and it measures customer retention by that share.

response: positioned GTF as sole geared architecture
doc: Paris Air Show Investor Meeting (Special Call)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We're still the only company in the world that's got a geared turbofan architecture. We're the only company in the world with a fifth-generation fighter engine.
finding: P&W presented the geared architecture as a unique technical differentiator against rival engine makers in 2017.

trigger: rising aircraft-on-ground numbers among A320neo GTF operators
response: negotiated reallocation of engines from Airbus line to lease pool
speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: What we are working right now with Airbus is to see whether we want to reallocate or change the mix between engines that go towards new aircraft versus what goes into the lease pool this year to support the engines in the fields better at this point in time.
finding: In mid-September P&W was already negotiating with Airbus to shift GTFs from new aircraft to the lease/spares pool; the decision followed within weeks.

trigger: Airbus takeover of the Bombardier CSeries
response: claimed it as validation of GTF technology
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: it was a validation of the Geared Turbofan, because the GTF, as you guys know, is the sole source engine on the CSeries. And despite all that's been written about the durability issues, blah, blah, blah, the fact is the engine works and Airbus has high confidence or they wouldn't have done this deal.
finding: P&W read Airbus's CSeries takeover as a vote of confidence in its sole-source GTF position and played down the durability issues.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: Airbus has talked about going through rate 63. ... they've talked about going to rate 70 or even potentially a rate 75. That's really difficult. ... Or is this simply a 3-year spike, and do you really want to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in capacity for what might be 3 or 4 years of additional production?
finding: P&W resisted funding capacity for Airbus rates of 70-75 unless the demand was durable, not a 3-4 year spike.
trigger: Airbus ambition to raise A320neo rate to 70-75/month
response: support Airbus but question the capacity investment

speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: you may have seen that the Indian authorities took a decision to ground the fleet in India that have engines of this that had the design escape. We're disappointed with that decision, but I can tell you that by the end of April, that fleet will be back up in the air flying in India.
finding: When India's regulator grounded affected A320neos, P&W committed to getting the fleet back in the air within about two months.
response: rework and return to service by end of April

speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: since the Paris Air Show last year, we sold about 650 airplanes worth of GTFs, roughly 500 of those were NEOs, and the balance were split between Embraer, Bombardier and Aircoupe. ... very proud of the Delta award. Delta is a very technically astute airline
finding: Despite 2017 execution problems P&W booked about 650 aircraft of GTF orders in nine months, including Delta.

speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: I'm not going to tell you what our GTF deliveries are in 2018 and I'm not going to tell you that because you know my negative engine margin number. If I give you the volume, you can calculate the average loss per engine and so can my competitor. ... in the next 3 years, we will deliver over 2,500 GTFs
finding: P&W withheld annual GTF delivery counts so CFM could not calculate its average OE loss per engine, disclosing only 2,500+ deliveries over three years.
trigger: rival CFM able to infer P&W per-engine pricing
response: withhold annual delivery counts

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: we're at about a rate 55 for engines today. We have spoken to Airbus. We know that there's a desire to increase that. And we are committed to take that rate up over the next couple of years, but I think there's a question beyond that, whether or not the sub-tier suppliers really have the capacity.
finding: P&W committed to follow Airbus's A320neo rate increases from about rate 55 over two years but questioned going further on sub-tier supplier capacity.
trigger: Airbus desire to raise A320neo production rates
response: committed to a measured ramp while flagging supply-chain limits
lag: over the next couple of years

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: we actually backed off from some of the campaigns because, at that time, the only way we could have won those campaigns when there was a cloud of doubt to some extent, was through pricing. And we didn't want to do that. ... the market share has been lower because we deliberately backed off.
finding: While durability doubts hung over the GTF, P&W chose to lose A320neo campaigns rather than win them on price, accepting a lower share.
trigger: durability doubts about the GTF during engine campaigns
response: withdrew from price-driven campaigns and accepted lower share

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: if you go back and look at since Paris Air Show to now, our market share is 56% on the engines that have selected. Airlines like Delta, airlines like JetBlue, very sophisticated technical shops, have put their confidence in the GTF.
finding: P&W said it had won 56% of A320neo engine selections since the 2017 Paris Air Show, including Delta and JetBlue.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: we continue to work with Airbus and continue to work with the supply chain to see if we can ramp up even more quickly, but that will take additional capital and additional time, but we'll work through that. ... I think if there's another big ramp up in production beyond what we see today, it will be a challenge
finding: When Airbus pushed for faster A320neo rates, P&W agreed to explore it but flagged that more rate needs more capital and time.
trigger: Airbus seeking faster A320neo production ramp
response: work on it with the supply chain, but only with additional capital and time

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: the airlines have been relatively patient with us because we can tell them when they're going to have the removals. We've got lots of spare engines out there. And we're doing the best to minimize disruptions. Having said that, there are a number of AOG aircraft out there, about 10 today as we speak.
finding: P&W managed GTF durability removals by forecasting them for airlines and flooding the fleet with spare engines, keeping aircraft-on-ground to about ten.
response: predictable removal forecasts and a large spare engine pool

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: There's 2 big bottlenecks... One is on the casting side... The second place is our own forging capacity down in Georgia. And we just added a fifth line down there... that fifth press is almost fully utilized... a couple of constraints out there that require, I would say, a lot of CapEx and probably a couple of years.
finding: When asked whether the A320neo/GTF could win share while the 737 MAX was grounded and a rival engine had blade issues, UTC said castings and its own forging capacity capped any extra ramp; more output would need significant capex and about two years.
trigger: 737 MAX grounding and CFM LEAP blade controversy (analyst)
response: No extra ramp beyond plan; capacity needs capex and ~2 years

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: a ramp up beyond -- I think, today, we're building at about 6th rate, 65... It's probably a 2- to 2.5-year process, right? To add additional forging capacity at our Georgia forge operations at least 2 years... you're not going to see us be able to step up with a lot more deliveries.
finding: Asked whether a long 737 MAX grounding could let GTF output rise, Hayes said P&W was capped at about rate 65 and that more forging and casting capacity would take 2-2.5 years, so P&W could not quickly take advantage of Boeing's problem.
trigger: Extended 737 MAX grounding (possible shift of demand to A320neo)
response: No near-term GTF output increase

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: This week, we'll announce over 1,000 new engine orders in the large commercial engine business... That will put us at a backlog of over 10,000 engines... It took 33 years for us to get 7,000 engine orders on the V2500. It's taken us 9 years to get north of 10,000 orders on the engine.
finding: The GTF passed 10,000 engine orders in 9 years (versus 7,000 V2500 orders in 33 years), which P&W used as evidence of a durable market position.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: I will tell you that, that decision was completely economically based. It was all about price... This was not a conversation about the technical capability, the engine or the availability in engines, it was a conversation about price.
finding: P&W attributed losing IndiGo's 2019 engine decision to price alone, denying that GTF durability or availability played a role, despite the airline's known GTF groundings.
trigger: IndiGo engine selection (2019) going against P&W
response: Declined to match price; publicly framed loss as price-only

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: Pratt & Whitney, they booked nearly 1,000 GTF firm and option orders at the Paris Air Show. And the Pratt team continues to execute on the GTF cost reduction initiatives and importantly, are meeting the customer delivery requirements.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)

finding: In 2019 P&W commercial engines carried over $1.2B a year of negative engine margin plus nearly $1B of R&D, a low-single-digit-margin business that depends on the 2024-25 aftermarket ramp.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)

But the absolute level of E&D, we expect to remain relatively flat as we look to continue to stay ahead of the curve.
finding: P&W keeps E&D flat in absolute terms between programmes and steps it up only when a brand-new engine programme is launched.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)

finding: UTC saw the Raytheon merger as making a big engine investment (e.g. a new programme) easier to fund than for a standalone commercial aerospace company, while promising capital discipline.

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO (UTC)

finding: Below free cash flow, P&W's recurring investing outflows (payments to Rolls-Royce, spare-engine lease pools and customer financing) ran at $1-1.5B in 2019, falling below $1B later, and the Rolls-Royce payments end after 2027.

speaker: Carroll Lane, VP Investor Relations (UTC)

finding: P&W re-estimates long-term service contract costs fleet by fleet and books the adjustments; ageing PW4000 fleets needed higher-cost repairs, which dented 2019 aftermarket growth.

finding: P&W's F135 military engine backlog grew by more than $7B in late 2019, a defense cushion for the commercial business.

finding: In 2019 P&W grew profit as V2500 production wound down and GTF shipments rose, helped by lower E&D spending.

finding: After five years of adding overhead to ramp the GTF, P&W began cutting (over 1,000 early retirements in Q4 2019) even before COVID, as a new president took over.

Operating profit benefited from drop-through on higher military sales, continued GTF cost reduction, lower E&D and a customer settlement. ... finding: About half of P&W's business is aftermarket, which makes its profit and cash highly sensitive to flying hours.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO

finding: RTX spends about $2.5B a year on commercial aero E&D, and P&W took two-thirds (about $300M) of the 20% COVID cut, showing its R&D budget flexes with the cycle.
response: 20% cut to commercial aero E&D

quote: The biggest obviously is the V2500, as you know, and there's about 7,000 engines that we've sold. About 6,000 of those are still in active service. You, of course, got the GTF, which isn't really contributing much in terms of aftermarket today in terms of profit. ... The V accounts are about 50% of the aftermarket today.
finding: In 2020 the V2500 (about 6,000 active engines) provided half of P&W's aftermarket while the GTF contributed little aftermarket profit yet.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: on the GTF, obviously, as everybody knows, we lose money every time we ship an engine. And so there's actually good news from the lower production on the GTF. That is offset somewhat by the lack of absorption. ... You're taking 5% to 10% of the cost out every year. That's going to be slower as volumes go down.
finding: P&W sells every GTF at a loss (negative OE margin) and depends on 5-10% annual cost reduction down the learning curve, so lower volume both saves OE losses and slows cost-down.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So overall, you're probably going to get about $100 million of pickup as a result of the lower volumes on GTF. But I think that's a -- it's a relatively modest number because of the absorption impact.
finding: COVID's cut to GTF deliveries saved P&W only about $100M of OE losses in 2020 because factory under-absorption offset most of it.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: many of the aftermarket contracts that we have on the Pratt side are hours-based. So even if planes aren't flying full, if they're flying, they're generating revenue, they're generating aftermarket. ... So I think about 70% probably of the Pratt fleet today is powered by the hour.
finding: About 70% of the P&W fleet was on power-by-the-hour contracts, so aftermarket revenue follows flying hours rather than passenger loads.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: The other 25 -- another 25% is related to, let's call it, the legacy PW4000, PW2000 programs. ... That -- again, it's highly profitable, and that is the part that I think we are most concerned about in terms of how many of those planes are going to return to service.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO

finding: P&W's aftermarket fell from +4% in Q1 2020 to -75% in April, and RTX planned on about -50% for the rest of 2020.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO

finding: COVID made RTX stretch its $18-20B capital return from 3 to 4 years, with the dividend as first priority and buybacks second.
response: capital return period extended from 3 to 4 years

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO

finding: Military work gave Pratt and Collins a partial hedge, just under 30% of 2019 sales and still growing in 2020.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO

response: E&D and capex cuts

finding: The V2500 (IAE) was about half of P&W's large commercial engine aftermarket in 2020, a young fleet of about 6,000 engines with much of its shop-visit revenue still to come.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: we do have some wide-body exposure on the PW2000 and PW4000 engines. Combined, that's about 20% to 25% of Pratt's aftermarket. ... And margins are normally more healthy, if you will, for a fully learned out engine, but given the age of the fleet, there's also other alternatives around used material that's available, discounted maintenance programs
finding: Mature, fully learned-out engines like the PW2000/PW4000 earn P&W the healthiest aftermarket margins, but late in life that margin is eroded by used material and discounted maintenance programmes.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: And then the balance of the aftermarket, the remaining roughly 25%, is made up of the GP7000, the GTF and some other overhaul work. Lower margins here, think more wrench-turning. And then the GTF, of course, is still in the retrofit and warranty phase.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: if you take 4 years of dividends, just directionally, that would be about $12 billion. And that would leave $6 billion to $8 billion for share buybacks that would likely occur primarily in years 3 and 4 ... we do not need large-scale M&A as we already have the size, scale and technologies.
finding: RTX's capital allocation after the merger was roughly $12B of dividends plus $6-8B of buybacks over 4 years, and it ruled out large-scale M&A.

finding: At the Q2 2020 trough P&W commercial OE fell 42% and aftermarket 51%, with legacy shop visits down 64% while the GTF aftermarket still grew.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, VP FP&A and IR

finding: P&W swung to a $151M operating loss in Q2 2020 because its profit depends on aftermarket volume; lower GTF deliveries slightly reduced negative engine margin.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: you've got about $200 million of E&D actions. You think about $100 million of discretionary spend and the other $300 million was really employee-related. ... on the commercial aerospace, it reduced about 8,000 positions. Some of those will come back with volume. Some of them will be permanently reduced.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: because when you look at that, you're talking $400 million in the aggregate, roughly $200 million in each of the 2 segments. And then on top of that, you mentioned the bankruptcies, right? I'm probably off, but it was at least 5 in the quarter

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: when we just originally we're going to have about a 10% to 12% reduction in SG&A at Pratt, Chris Calio came to me a month or so ago and said, "This is tougher than what we had thought. We're going to need to take more folks out."

But those are not big acquisitions. ... it would be well less than $0.5 billion in total spending this year, so no big M&A.

quote: we set aggressive targets in the first quarter to reduce cost by about $2 billion and to take actions to conserve about $4 billion of cash. We're taking the difficult but necessary actions to reduce headcount at both Collins and Pratt. We'll reduce about 20% of our commercial aero headcount; that's about 15,000 positions.

So in a, I would say, to be very cautious, focus on safety first, we're doing some accelerated inspections and accelerated retrofit
finding: After in-flight shutdowns at IndiGo and GoAir, P&W responded with accelerated inspections and blade retrofits, prioritising safety over cost.
trigger: GTF in-flight shutdowns in India from fractured third-stage turbine blades
response: accelerated inspections and retrofit of old-design blades
lag: retrofit mostly in H1 2020, complete by end-2020

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: the combustor liner, which has been a problem since the get-go, especially in these difficult operating environments ... The latest version of the combustor, the D, will be out sometime in the, I think, June time frame this year ... So no new issues. But I'll tell you it's causing a lot of the operators pain, especially in India and China
finding: The GTF combustor liner had been a durability problem from entry into service, and P&W admitted the retrofit programme was causing operators real pain, especially in hot, harsh environments.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, Acting CFO
quote: When we came out of the fourth quarter here, very strong inductions. So we saw about a 6% increase quarter-over-quarter in induction activity on the V. ... And with the 737 MAX situation, the legacy planes are flying quite a bit more.
finding: Boeing's 737 MAX grounding kept older aircraft flying and lifted V2500 shop visits for P&W before COVID.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: At Pratt, the GTF engine program achieved 2 significant milestones as the first in-service GTF engine exceeded 10,000 service hours. And more importantly, the program reached 5 million revenue flight hours across the combined GTF-powered fleet.
finding: By Q1 2020 the lead GTF engine had passed 10,000 service hours and the fleet 5 million revenue flight hours, which P&W offered as evidence of maturing durability.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: The DoD raised it from 80% to 90%. We've pushed all that cash, about $450 million, in the last 2 months out to our suppliers to make sure that they can maintain their financial viability. ... it is the small business suppliers that I'm most worried about.
finding: RTX passed about $450M of accelerated defense progress payments to suppliers in COVID, seeing small suppliers as the biggest risk to its production base.
response: passed about $450M of progress payments through to suppliers

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: We typically would expect about 1,000 engine inductions a year on the V. Maybe a little bit north of that. So that's roughly 80, 85 a month. And we saw that rate, January, February and it's really to the last week of March. And I think in April itself, it was down like 75%, to 25, 26 engines.
finding: The V2500 normally generates about 1,000 shop visits a year for P&W, and inductions fell 75% in April 2020.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: we now expect both Pratt and Collins to experience negative operating profit in Q2 as repair intake and shop visit inductions are significantly reduced. We're seeing under-absorption in our factories being realized ... they're down anywhere from 60% to 70% for Pratt engine inductions
finding: Loss of shop-visit inductions (down 60-70%) and factory under-absorption pushed P&W into operating losses in Q2 2020.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: A lot of our supply chain have long lead times, so think 12 to 18 months. ... And we're also balancing the health of the supply base ... when we come out of this -- and again, it's not a matter of if, it's when, we need our supply base there with us. So it is a balancing act. The UTC aero, the legacy business and their inventory turns last year, they turned about 4x.
finding: P&W and Collins kept taking supplier deliveries through the COVID collapse to protect the supply base for the recovery, accepting billions of excess inventory because of 12-18 month lead times.
trigger: sudden OE rate cuts in COVID
response: keep supporting suppliers, accept inventory build

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: What we are doing is we are utilizing available -- what is now available shop capacity to fix the issues in the fleet this year, right? ... Our goal is to have the majority of the GTF engines to be at that latest configuration with the enhancements and the improvements by the end of the year
finding: P&W used COVID's spare shop capacity to fix GTF durability issues, aiming to bring most GTF engines to the latest configuration by end-2020.
trigger: GTF durability issues over its first 5 million flight hours; COVID freed shop capacity
response: accelerated GTF retrofit to latest configuration

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: if you think about the large commercial aftermarket, it was down about 55%, and that was really led -- of course, PW2000 was way down, like 80%. The V was down like 60%. So -- and GTF was actually not down.
finding: In Q2 2020 P&W's aftermarket collapse was concentrated in older fleets (PW2000 -80%, V2500 -60%) while the young GTF aftermarket held up.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we're extremely confident in the GTF program. We continue to do the durability upgrades. And even in the midst of the pandemic, we see roughly 75% of the A320neo powered or GTF-powered fleet flying. That's up from 65%. And if you look at the A220, the old CSeries, that's being reused roughly 85%.
finding: P&W kept doing GTF durability upgrades through COVID, and GTF-powered A320neo and A220 fleets flew at higher rates than older fleets.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: At Pratt, we see third quarter V2500 inductions into the engine center. That's down about 60% and in line with what we saw in Q2. So we're only seeing about 30 shop visits a month versus the 90 that we had seen last year.
finding: V2500 shop visits fell from about 90 to 30 a month in 2020, cutting the cash aftermarket from P&W's mature narrowbody fleet.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Fortunately, we don't have a lot of engines out there on the widebody. Those are old PW4000 fleet that was on some 330s and some early 777s and 47s. We expect most of those to be retired during the course of the next couple of years.
finding: P&W had almost no widebody exposure left, only an ageing PW4000 fleet it expected to retire within a couple of years, and treated that as a benefit in the downturn.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: The good news is, as we continue to ship GTF-powered aircraft, we're replacing the fleet of retired engines faster, but we're actually adding more to the fleet than the retirements coming out.
finding: P&W's installed base was still growing in 2020 because GTF deliveries outpaced retirements of old engines.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we expected to hit full rate production early next year. And that's now been pushed out as both -- well, specifically on the A320 and the A220 fleet, we've seen those reduced by about 40%.
finding: COVID pushed back GTF full-rate production (planned for early 2021) as A320neo and A220 rates fell about 40%.
trigger: Airbus A320 and A220 production cuts of about 40%
response: GTF full-rate production pushed out

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: The learning curve that we had expected is about 88%, so a 12% reduction every time you double volume. And we have been on that curve since really the inception of the program. Obviously, we're still on the curve. It's just going to take longer because the volume is not there
finding: P&W plans GTF production cost on an 88% learning curve (12% cost cut per doubling of volume) and said COVID only delays progress along it.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we're strategically utilizing available shop capacity to upgrade the GTF fleet to the latest configuration to ensure our customers' fleets are healthy and well positioned as we exit the year and demand slowly returns.
finding: P&W used idle COVID shop capacity to retrofit the GTF installed base to the latest (durability) configuration, turning the downturn into a fleet-upgrade window.
trigger: COVID-driven slump in shop visits leaving spare capacity
response: upgrade GTF fleet to latest configuration

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Pratt's shop visits in the quarter, right, down about 55%. Now that's a little bit better than what we saw in the second quarter, which is down 64%, but that's going to take a long time to get back to the 2019 levels.
finding: P&W legacy shop visits fell 64% in Q2 2020 and 55% in Q3, and management expected a long climb back to 2019 levels.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Obviously, the GTF, not so much. We haven't -- we still got our arms around that. And even on the V, I mean you're still -- they're still flying that plane. It's still one of the more efficient. So not a big concern of serviceable material on the Pratt side today
finding: P&W saw little threat from used serviceable material to its GTF and V2500 aftermarket because it controls GTF material and the V2500 fleet was still flying.

finding: RTX plans on a 6-9 month lag between traffic recovery and aftermarket recovery, with traffic back to 2019 in 2023.

doc: Baird Industrial Conference, Nov 2020 (Company Conference Presentation)

finding: P&W expected used serviceable material and green-time management to hit its older PW2000/PW4000 aftermarket most and its younger V2500/GTF fleets least.

finding: By end-2020 the GTF fleet reached 7.5M hours and 99.97% dispatch reliability, and P&W presented its utilisation through COVID as proof of the engine's value.

speaker: Toby O'Brien, CFO (RTX)
quote: we previously took the difficult action to reduce commercial headcount at Collins and Pratt by 15,000 and to eliminate 4,000 contractor roles... reducing our total commercial aero headcount now by approximately 20%. And as you've heard, we announced Pratt's investment in the new airfoil facility
finding: RTX cut commercial aero headcount by about 20% in COVID while still funding P&W's new airfoil plant.

doc: Cowen A&D Conference, Feb 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Toby O'Brien, CFO (RTX)
quote: the airfoil facility, it's a couple, 3 years away, right, and before we get to full volume. So we'll start -- that $175 million won't start -- it won't be at full rate in 2023 as we ramp up the facility, but it will build up over the next several years beyond that.
finding: The Asheville airfoil plant, committed during COVID, pays back only from about 2023 onward, a multi-year structural bet.

doc: Barclays Industrial Select Conference, Feb 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)

finding: By early 2021 P&W had retrofitted about 96% of the GTF fleet and declared its teething durability problems behind it.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: Pratt & Whitney accelerated upgrades to the geared turbofan engine, and we shifted resources across the business to keep production lines rolling.
finding: In 2020 P&W pulled GTF upgrades forward during the downturn and kept production lines running.

As a result, there are about 20 aircraft today that are sitting there that do not have a serviceable engine.
finding: P&W under-invested in F135 sustainment capacity, leaving about 20 F-35s without serviceable engines; it committed to add equipment to recover by end-2021.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: about 118 Vs into the shop in the first quarter, which is exactly on plan... only about 60% of the V fleet is flying... compare that to the GTF-powered fleet, which is in the high 80s... We're not going to get back to 1,000 engines this year, probably not for 2 more years on the V.
finding: In early 2021 only about 60% of the V2500 fleet flew against the high 80s% for GTF aircraft; P&W expected V2500 shop visits to take about two years to regain 1,000 a year.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: if you think about Pratt's installed base of 11,000-plus engines or so, about 10% of that is freighters. Those rolled PW4000, those are the 94-inch 767s and 747s. That has actually been a pleasant surprise... the older stuff is still out there. It's still a meaningful piece of the aftermarket. I think it's like 20% -- 25%.
finding: Freighter use of legacy PW4000s supported P&W's aftermarket in 2021; legacy widebody engines were still about 20-25% of the aftermarket.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: Sole source on the top priority programs, bomber, mobility, fighter... When we look at our long-term planning horizon, we see delivering about 150 of these a year plus power modules... That will be worth around $11 billion in sales, '21 through '25.
finding: P&W's sole-source military franchises, chiefly about 150 F135s a year (about $11B of 2021-25 sales), give it a steady base alongside commercial.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: 10,000 engines in its base today, 80% of those serve the narrow-body segment, led, of course, by the V2500 on the CEO, the GTF dual source on the NEO and then sole source on the A220 and the Embraer E2 platform... It's a very young fleet. 50% is less than 10 years old.
finding: P&W's large commercial engine base is narrowbody-focused and young (V2500, GTF dual-source on the A320neo, sole-source on the A220 and E2).

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: 80% of those planes are operating today. I think utilization is about 90% of pre-pandemic... in the order book, 40% low-cost carriers, those that have actually really well positioned themselves coming out of this pandemic and another 30%, what I would call traditional network like the Lufthansas and the Deltas of the world.
finding: GTF operators kept flying through COVID (80% active, 90% utilisation), and the backlog is 40% low-cost carriers.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: about 1/3, serve the cargo market. In fact, we've seen many of the PW2000 and 4000 operators approach us about extending the life of those. I think there's durable strength in the cargo market
finding: Cargo demand kept P&W's widebody legacy engines (PW2000/PW4000) in service, with operators asking for life extensions.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We've added a new combustor and some other things to increase the durability of the engine... didn't take our foot off the accelerator on GTF, MRO, continued to put engines to the shop. Those are investments, as you know, because they're not margin contributing... we see this turning the corner in about that 24-month time frame.
finding: P&W absorbed loss-making GTF shop visits during COVID to fix fleet durability (new combustor) and expected the GTF aftermarket to turn profitable in about two years.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: This is our new facility in Asheville, North Carolina, vertically integrated advanced airfoils. It will provide the airfoils for the GTF and the F135. As many of you are all too aware, this is a very constrained, very expensive value stream... it will produce about $180 million in annual savings
finding: P&W vertically integrated turbine-airfoil production (Asheville) to secure a constrained, costly supply chain for the GTF and F135 and save about $180M a year.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: we had to ramp up the inventory story, a, for the actual production ramp; and b, because we had a lot of earlier visits than we thought, right? So we needed to bring in that inventory as well. As these time on wing upgrades take hold, time on wing and the maintenance interval grows, that will recede.
finding: Early GTF shop visits (poor durability) forced P&W to carry extra inventory, which it expected to fall as time-on-wing upgrades took hold.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: we're in that 500, 550 sort of shop visit range this year. We see a 50% increase through 2025. We're going to push to try to get it back to 1,000. You may have heard a few years ago, it was going to be 1,000 shop visits a year for the next 7 years.
finding: Change of position: the pre-COVID plan of about 1,000 V2500 shop visits a year was cut to about 525 in 2021 rising 50% by 2025.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: shop visits increasing by about 50% from where we expect them to be this year in 2021. So it put you in the range of about 800 or so V2500 shop visits. That's obviously a bit lower than what we were thinking prepandemic. We were thinking about 1,000 shop visits in that time period.
finding: COVID cut P&W's mid-decade V2500 shop-visit outlook from about 1,000 a year to about 800.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: We were really able to take advantage of shop visit activity that was down last year to bring in GTFs and overhaul. I'd say we're nearly 99% complete with retrofitting a couple of the issues that we were facing. We still have an option to upgrade the combustor... That will improve time on wing as well.
finding: P&W used the COVID lull in shop visits to bring GTFs in and retrofit nearly all of the fleet's early durability fixes, with a combustor upgrade still to come to extend time on wing.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: the engine is performing great, dispatch reliability of 99.97% between the A320, A220 and Embraer models. We've got over 9 million hours of time on these engines.
finding: By mid-2021 the GTF fleet reached 99.97% dispatch reliability and 9M+ hours across the A320neo, A220 and E2.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: At Pratt, we continue to build on the overhaul capability and drive turnaround time across our geared turbofan network. The team has made good progress this year, demonstrated a 15% turnaround time improvement over the past year. But importantly, they're on track to drive a 30% reduction by the end of this year.
finding: P&W kept investing in GTF MRO capacity through the downturn, targeting a 30% cut in shop turnaround time by end-2021.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: we do see OE volumes going up in the 2025 time period. And the Pratt & Whitney team is aggressively working cost reduction actions to contain that negative engine margin at an appropriate level.
finding: P&W's response to rising GTF OE volumes is to cut cost to contain negative engine margin, not to reprice.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: what we didn't do is close a lot of factories or eliminate a lot of capacity... at Pratt, from a cost standpoint, is we've got all this unabsorbed overhead... we're still facilitized to do 1,000 of these... This year, we'll probably do 550 of these overhauls, but the capacity still exists. It's the same on the GTF.
finding: P&W kept its V2500 and GTF overhaul capacity through COVID, accepting unabsorbed overhead so it could serve a rebound.

finding: V2500 shop inductions are the main driver of P&W's aftermarket; about 145-150 visits a quarter in Q3 2021, with spare orders up 25%.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: the GTF, today, we've got just [ over ] 900 aircraft delivered. We've flown about 9.5 million hours. We've got a [ 99.9% ] dispatch reliability rate. The engine is great. And we continue to see opportunities to grow our market position on the A320.
finding: By October 2021 P&W claimed the GTF's early reliability problems were behind it (900+ aircraft, 9.5M hours, 99.9% dispatch) and sought to grow A320neo share.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: while we have good coverage under long-term agreements, we've seen lead times double on some of these raw materials.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: So as you think about going down from roughly, what, 16 engines a month down to 13 engines a month, it will have an impact on Pratt... let's call it, $10 million in engine, so you're going to lose $30 million a month. So you may lose $350 million, $360 million of revenue going forward.
finding: The F-35 rate cut from 16 to 13 engines a month costs P&W about $350M a year of revenue at about $10M per F135.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: On the Pratt side, very good shop visit induction. We saw 49% year-over-year legacy shop visits come in. That's a little higher than the 30%, 35% that we thought we would see. So that upside, probably about $75 million of sales, is contributing to a full year $100 million increase in the Pratt outlook
finding: Legacy (mainly V2500) shop visits recovered faster than planned in Q3 2021, and that aftermarket upside drove P&W's outlook raise.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: Narrow-body is all good. That's operating -- [ A320 ] fleet out there is operating about 80% of pre-COVID, similar like 70% on the V2500 fleet.
finding: By late 2021 the A320 fleet was flying at about 80% of pre-COVID levels and the V2500 fleet at about 70%, underpinning P&W's aftermarket recovery.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: The engine is performing very, very well. The platform of engines have flown nearly 11 million hours with a dispatch reliability, well over 99%. The fleet remained highly utilized even through the panic So we're talking 87%, 88% utilization. And even the V fleet is at 70% utilization.
finding: In late 2021 P&W presented the GTF as reliable and heavily used (87-88% utilisation), with the V2500 fleet at 70%.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: in our supply chain, we see some labor shortages with skilled positions. And I can think of probably the most important one right now is in the castings where we see a shortage of welders... We see that we're going to have a slow Q1, as Neil said, primarily at Pratt
finding: The castings shortage that limited GTF deliveries through 2022 was first flagged in January 2022 as a lack of skilled welders at suppliers.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: to date, on the GTF program, we have had more than 12 million flight hours on that. In the last 12 months, dispatch reliability has been 99.96%. So I know that we had a lot of teething problems back in '16 and '17... it impacted some of our time on wing, impacted some of those maintenance support contracts.
finding: In January 2022 RTX defended its GTF maintenance contracts, citing 12M flight hours and 99.96% dispatch reliability and treating the 2016-17 teething problems that hurt time on wing as past.
trigger: analyst concern on GTF time on wing and contract pricing
response: defended contract pricing citing 99.96% dispatch reliability

quote: One, obviously, was fuel burn. That was a 15% benefit over the V2500. We clearly achieved that. What we did not achieve, I would say, in the first few years of delivery... was a robust engine. We had teething problems, as we've talked about, primarily around the combustor and primarily in some of the more difficult environment environments like India.
finding: RTX admitted the early GTF met its 15% fuel-burn goal but not durability, with combustor problems especially in harsh environments such as India.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: that impacted the aftermarket as we brought those engines back, sometimes within a year or 2 of shipping them to update the combustor. Right now, I would tell you the combustors there are lasting at least 10,000 hours now, which is good news.

finding: P&W told investors early that it would miss about 70 Airbus engines in Q1 2022 because of castings, and promised a catch-up later in the year.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we had a problem with our structural casting supplier, where we were not able to get castings into our MRP schedule. That resulted in about 70 engines moving out of the first quarter. That problem is not behind us, but we are working with that supplier to recover that.
finding: One casting supplier caused P&W to miss about 70 engine deliveries in Q1 2022; P&W worked with the supplier rather than switch.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: And similarly at Pratt, we now expect commercial OE to be up low teens. I had talked about -- Greg and I had talked about OE shipments being up about 200. Think about that now as about up 180 at the Pratt business year-over-year.
finding: Russia and castings cut P&W's planned 2022 increase in engine shipments from about 200 to about 180.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we started advanced purchasing back in the fourth quarter when we were able to get ahead of some of the sanctions. So we have inventory for a big chunk of that throughout -- through the end of this year... Russia accounted for about 15% of global sponge production.
finding: RTX pre-bought Russian titanium in Q4 2021, anticipating sanctions, covering most 2022 needs; Pratt Canada deliveries still slipped.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So those are primarily titanium castings from a -- from our supplier that's impacting. These are structural castings, which means you can't really build -- start building most of the engine until you get the castings in
finding: The GTF bottleneck was titanium structural castings needed before most of the engine can be built, so one part stopped whole-engine output.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: We've talked about castings and the impact that that's had to Pratt & Whitney, particularly on the large commercial engine deliveries there. We have a recovery plan... With that comes some higher engine deliveries here in the second quarter with some higher negative engine margin.
finding: P&W's casting recovery meant more engine deliveries and therefore more negative engine margin, so catching up on OE hurts near-term profit.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: So just to be clear, the casting issue is one that's a domestic supplier, and it's really been around timeliness and quality.
finding: P&W's 2022 GTF delivery shortfall came from one domestic structural-castings supplier with timeliness and quality problems, a single-source weakness.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: Yes, particularly on the V2500. Customers, over the last couple of years, were doing more minimalist overhauls conserving their cash, rightfully so. But now we see higher content per shop visit as those airlines are doing a more robust, more full overhaul.
finding: Airlines deferred V2500 work with minimal overhauls during COVID and switched back to full overhauls in 2022, raising P&W's revenue per shop visit.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: I think the PW2000s, the average age is like 27 years. The retirement rate there is more in the 4% to 5% range, whereas -- I didn't address this, but on the Vs, we're talking 1%, 1.5%, very low recent retirement rates.
finding: P&W's legacy fleets retire slowly (V2500 1-1.5% a year, PW2000 4-5%), extending aftermarket tails.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Microelectronics, rocket motors, structural castings, all continue to pace manufacturing lines. Today, we have people embedded about 330 of our suppliers to help improve performance. And we're also qualifying second, in some cases, third sources for critical parts as necessary.
finding: RTX's response to supplier bottlenecks (including P&W structural castings) was to embed staff at suppliers and qualify second and third sources.
response: staff embedded at ~330 suppliers; second/third sources qualified

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Now it doesn't always work. We talked about structural castings at Pratt & Whitney back in Q1. That continues to be a challenge.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: right now, we continue to deliver GTFs behind schedule. And we will not catch up, as I think I said back in February, until the end... of the year. And this is -- again, goes back to a single issue around structural castings. We're not holding up the line at Airbus.
finding: P&W delivered GTFs late through 2022 because of structural castings but prioritised keeping the Airbus A320neo and A220 lines moving.
response: manage deliveries with customers; catch up by year-end

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: And Asheville, while it is a large facility, the actual number of employees is only I think about 800 that we're going to be hiring, and we have been actively hiring them today to train them for the opening, which has happened sometime I think at the end of next year.
finding: P&W was building a new highly automated airfoil plant (Asheville) with about 800 staff, opening around end-2023.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we're also making sure that we have assured supply chain. So we're looking to make sure we have second sources outside of China in the case that the geopolitical tensions rise to the point where we're not able to access that supply chain there.
