quote: Will we get to breakeven? I don't see that. Even the V2500, which we've built for 30 years was still a negative margin business going out the door at the end of its production run... in terms of negative engine margin in total, that's peak last year, it won't go up any higher than that
finding: P&W accepts that narrowbody OE engines are sold at a loss for the whole production run (as with the V2500), unlike MTU's breakeven view; total GTF negative engine margin peaked in 2018.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: These are the company jewels that we're talking about being able to share. And you don't share those through JVs. You spread risk, you spread investment through JVs, but you don't share technologies.
finding: RTX's stated view of joint ventures: use them to share risk and investment, never to share core technology. This bears on any P&W participation in a partner's engine JV.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: You've been incredibly patient with us as we've gone through a very heavy investment period, both in terms of E&D, in terms of negative margin. And you've been so patient with us I want to start to paint the picture that you're going to get your reward, it's right in front of us.
finding: In 2019 P&W presented itself as leaving a heavy GTF investment period (E&D plus negative engine margin) and entering the harvest phase, a posture that argues against starting another large programme soon.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We derivatize engines. We do new set of lines on occasion, but then we just keep making derivatives after derivatives... So we do somewhere between 3 and 5 development programs a year, continually refresh our product line and capture more and more share.
finding: In small engines P&W prefers a derivative strategy (3-5 development programmes a year) over occasional clean-sheet engines.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: The wrench-turning, the actual labor and wrench-turning, you don't make margin on that. You make margin on the new parts, the used parts and the repaired parts. Our strategy has been to minimize our investment in our own infrastructure. Let third parties make that investment
finding: P&W's aftermarket model captures margin on parts (new, used, repaired) and leaves shop labour and MRO capex to third parties: of 5-6 new GTF shops by 2025, only one would be P&W-owned.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: It has the potential to deliver 30% in fuel savings. Now I will equate this to what I would say the gear was. So in early 2000, we've been talking about gear fans, gear threads and gear fans. Well, of course, it was 10 years until that actually went into service.
finding: P&W uses the geared fan's history (about 10+ years from early-2000s concept to service) as its benchmark for turning a new architecture into a product.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: No more negative engine headwind. E&D, flattish. But we're going to see this nice lift from aftermarket. Which means we're going to get more back towards what I would call our traditional return levels of that mid-teens number that we used to have before the big investment swing on the GTF.
finding: P&W's traditional through-cycle return level is mid-teens; the GTF investment swing depressed it and the plan was to return there by 2025 with flat E&D and no new negative-margin headwind.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: So we can absolutely get to 100%, there's no question about that. In terms of the power-by-the-hour, so there's really 2 types of contracts in power-by-the-hour. There's airlines that pay as they go, they pay us per flight hour; and there's airlines that actually will only pay at time of shop visits.
finding: P&W targets 100% free cash conversion by 2025 and runs two service contract types: pay-per-flight-hour and pay-at-shop-visit.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Paul Eremenko, SVP & CTO (UTC)
quote: you really can't just do this with a supplier relationship or a joint venture. There is a cardinal rule in engineering, and that is that the structure of the design team should mirror the architecture of the product.
finding: UTC's technology leadership argued that tightly integrated products need integrated teams rather than JVs or arm's-length supplier deals, a stance that makes an engine-core JV with a rival less natural.

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO (UTC)
quote: leased pool sales, I would say, is not something to rely on because if you think about it, the installed base will continue to grow. So the best way to think about that is that we won't necessarily add to the leased pool assets at the same rate that we have done in these first 2 years.
finding: P&W keeps and grows its spare-engine lease pool as the installed base grows, slowing additions after the first two ramp years rather than planning to sell pool assets.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: we have more to do on margins at Pratt. We have to invest in automation. We have to invest in the factories. We have to invest to take the cost down even further than what's laid out on these plans... taking full benefit of course for the GTF investments that we've made over the last 10 or 12 years.
finding: P&W planned further factory and automation investment to cut GTF cost below plan, and framed the GTF as a 10-12 year investment whose returns were now due.

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO (UTC)
quote: we generally have low to mid-teens returns on every engine campaign. That's our goal. But when I factor all of the investments in E&D and capital and everything else made, the GTF program overall is not a mid-teens return. It's above cost of capital, but it's more close to double-digit type of thing
finding: P&W targets low-to-mid-teens returns on each engine sales campaign, but the full GTF programme including E&D and capex returns only about 10%, above its cost of capital.

doc: UTC Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 2019)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: If it's a 2001-type downturn where the aviation industry is shut down, that's a bad thing on the commercial side. It's a good thing on the defense side... We have 10,000 GTF engines in backlog. The Boeing and Airbus have huge backlogs with the narrow-body, which is where we play mostly.
finding: Before COVID, UTC's downturn thesis relied on defence balancing commercial aerospace and on the 10,000-engine GTF narrowbody backlog; it recognised that an aviation shutdown would hurt the commercial side.

doc: UTC Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 2019)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: there is nothing else that we need to do in the RTX portfolio that would require a big M&A deal... our mission to be the world's preeminent supplier of aerospace and defense systems and be platform-agnostic in that, that says a lot. That says you're not going to go after a platform supplier.
finding: RTX positions itself as a platform-agnostic systems and engine supplier that will not buy or become an airframer, and saw no further big M&A as needed.

doc: UTC Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 2019)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: when you have an in-flight shutdown, that always raise the flag and say what's going on? And we stop. There is nothing more important than flight safety in aviation. So we'll be very cautious as we are with all of these incidents, evaluate them.
finding: P&W's stated rule for in-flight shutdowns is to stop and evaluate every incident cautiously, working with regulators, putting safety ahead of schedule.

doc: UTC Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 2019)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: They had been doing the maintenance themselves, and they were experiencing about 12,000 hours between overhauls, which is roughly 4 years. We brought the engines back into our shop under an FMP. We more than doubled the life of those engines... On an FMP where you're making money by the hour, not by the parts, usually profitable.
finding: P&W sees fleet-management (pay-per-hour) contracts as more profitable when its own shop and parts extend time between overhauls: it more than doubled V2500 on-wing life from about 12,000 hours for one airline.

speaker: Carroll Lane, VP Investor Relations (UTC)
quote: feeling very good about our cost takeout on the engine. That's clearly an ingredient to our success going forward. So I think overall and holistically, we're feeling good about our market share, good around the cost takeout, good around the profitability.
finding: P&W treats GTF unit-cost takeout as the key to programme success, alongside holding market share.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO (UTC)
quote: we did not participate in the bid because, quite frankly, a GTF, a gear does not work on a long-range business jet.
finding: P&W declines to bid where its architecture does not fit (the Gulfstream G700) rather than offer a non-geared product to chase share.
response: Did not bid

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: As you think about the XLR, the long-range version of the A321, that requires a higher-thrust engine, which we'll be able to deliver for Airbus and for their customers. And I can -- so we think more production go into the higher end, even just the basic A321, where Pratt has got probably a stronger offering.
finding: P&W positioned the GTF for the high-thrust end of the A320 family (A321, A321XLR), where it saw its offering as stronger than CFM's.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: We'll continue to take cost out, but we're trying to be judicious in terms of which customers we choose and which customers we elect not to make offerings to.
finding: Because each GTF was sold at a loss and capacity was tight, P&W chose which A320neo customers to bid for rather than chasing all share, the reverse of an aggressive-terms stance.
response: selective bidding on GTF campaigns

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: some of it is investable and some of it probably is not. ... And I think there will be places where we might elect not to invest and to cash out and other places where we may want to double down. ... we'll take a dispassionate look at the whole portfolio
finding: RTX planned a dispassionate post-merger portfolio review, choosing businesses to cash out versus double down on, which frames how P&W competes for capital.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Again, back in 2003, we saw about a 20% drop in the aftermarket for that -- for 2 quarters. I don't expect it's going to be that bad this time.
finding: In January 2020 RTX used the SARS precedent to expect little aftermarket impact from the coronavirus, an assumption the pandemic soon overturned.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: We're -- we do not anticipate any layoff. I think that would be the easiest thing to do, but quite frankly, given the scarcity of talented aerospace workers out there, we're not going to be laying anybody off for a 90-day delay here.
finding: Before COVID RTX refused to lay off workers for a short production pause because skilled aerospace labour was scarce, a stance it reversed months later with deep COVID headcount cuts.
response: no layoffs, work down backlog

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: The key is we don't want to cut the talent so deep that when the recovery happens, we don't have the right people. So we're trying to be judicious. ... we are actively working to try and take engineering talent and other talent that we've got in the legacy UTX business and move those folks over to programs on the Raytheon side.
finding: RTX tried to preserve engineering talent for the recovery by moving commercial aero engineers onto defense programmes instead of cutting them.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: With fuel prices as low as they are, the need for new aircraft is probably somewhat lessened, and people will probably fly some of the older, less efficient aircraft for a few more years to save on the capital of buying new airplanes
finding: RTX expects low fuel prices to delay airline demand for new, more efficient engines and extend the life of older fleets.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: About half of the Vs that are out there have not had its first major overhaul, and the other half have only had one. So if you think about it -- and you know the life cycle of these engines. You go through 2, sometimes 3 major overhauls. So we're still in the third inning, I would say, of the life of the V2500 in terms of the aftermarket.
finding: P&W models engine aftermarket value over 2-3 major overhauls per engine, and saw the 11-year-old V2500 fleet as early in that cycle with most of its aftermarket still to come.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: I think it's going to be a full 2 years before we see a recovery close to what we saw in terms of 2019 levels of aftermarket. And that could be -- it could well be 3 years. At the end of the day, we'll survive this. ... that is a relatively high-margin business, which affords us the opportunity to make these big investments in engines and other technologies across the portfolio.
finding: RTX says its high-margin aftermarket funds its big engine investments, so a 2-3 year aftermarket slump directly limits new engine investment capacity.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: it would have to be the deal of the century for us to think about M&A. But I would never say no if that rare opportunity were to present itself. And as you can imagine, not everybody's got the balance sheet that we have or the liquidity that we have. ... if we see a buying opportunity, we're not going to be shy. We're not going to be stupid either, though.
finding: In May 2020 RTX left the door open to opportunistic M&A in distressed commercial aerospace using its balance sheet, but by September it said there was no big M&A in its future.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: right now, we could see both the OE and aftermarket revenues down about 50% or so. ... where OE is down in line with the OEM production changes, and the aftermarket is generally down consistent with or in line with traffic. The recovery here clearly looks more like a U.
finding: RTX models commercial OE to track airframer production and aftermarket to track traffic, and in June 2020 expected a U-shaped recovery with both down about 50%.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: these actions, both the cost and cash are -- we're calibrating these to the demand in the current environment, including the input we're getting from conversations with our customers. And we still don't see a full recovery until sometime out in 2022.
finding: In June 2020 RTX expected full recovery by 2022, a view it pushed to 2023 by late July, showing its cost plans followed the shifting demand outlook.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: none of these actions here today contemplate shuttering of factories, closing of factories or anything of that nature there. They're all timing-related. Even the timing in variable -- even the E&D and CapEx reductions, while we won't just run out and restart projects, because we want to understand the viability of the ones that we're deferring, we will look to potentially reengage in those projects at an appropriate time if the business case around them still makes sense.
finding: In June 2020 RTX called its E&D and capex cuts deferrals, to be restarted only if each project's business case still held, and ruled out factory closures; by the autumn it was pursuing structural footprint changes, a shift in position.
response: defer E&D and capex projects; re-engage only if the business case holds

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we now would expect it will take at least until 2023 for commercial air traffic to recover to 2019 levels. As a result, we're evaluating what further actions and structural changes we need to make to our business to adjust for a prolonged recovery time line
finding: By July 2020 RTX had pushed its recovery assumption out to 2023 and responded by planning structural changes to its commercial aero businesses, P&W included.
trigger: pandemic proving worse than projected a few months earlier
response: evaluate further structural actions
lag: about 3 months after the April projection

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: in the quarter, we still invested $500 million in E&D on the commercial aero side. This is important as we think about the long term. We're not going to sacrifice long term for short term. We're going to take some tough cost actions.
finding: Even at the COVID trough RTX kept spending about $500M a quarter on commercial aero E&D, saying it would not sacrifice long-term technology for short-term savings.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: we need to take a look at some of the more structural costs that we have in our aerospace organization. That is cost in some high-cost manufacturing locations, what can we get after to restructure those businesses later this year. ... I think this is the opportunity to alter the overhead structure of the commercial aero businesses.
finding: RTX treated COVID as an opportunity to restructure high-cost manufacturing and overhead in its commercial aero businesses, not just to ride out the downturn.
response: plan structural restructuring of high-cost locations

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: if you think about closing a facility or moving a facility, it is a multiyear effort. The paybacks are generally pretty good to about 3 or 4 years for the investment. But you've got a lot of stakeholders to consider. You've got unions that have to be consulted.
finding: RTX sets a 3-4 year payback as the benchmark for footprint restructuring, acknowledging union and stakeholder constraints.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: What will happen, of course, as we've seen in prior downturns, is we will get a big slug of aftermarket, and these engines will all come back. They're time-based overhauls, and that should provide a bow wave of aftermarket activity once the airlines are back on their feet.
finding: RTX expected deferred engine overhauls to come back as a bow wave of aftermarket several years later, as in prior downturns.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Some of it will be in-sourcing work from the supply chain. Some of it will involve moving work from high-cost to lower-cost locations. Again, this is a multiyear program, but it's absolutely essential. We need the capacity because, eventually, demand will return. And I think by the time this comes online in late 2023
finding: P&W sizes capacity for the post-crisis recovery rather than the trough, in-sourcing supply-chain work and moving to low-cost locations with a multi-year lead time to late 2023.
response: build capacity for recovery; in-source and relocate to low-cost sites

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So we're going to use the advantage that we have to continue to gain market share, and we're also going to continue to invest. And I think, Ron, as you know, you have to invest for the long term. It takes 10 years to develop an engine.
finding: RTX treats engine development as a 10-year investment that must continue through downturns, and uses balance-sheet strength to keep investing while rivals retrench.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: what you're talking about from a commercial aerospace standpoint is probably a 2035 or so entry into service of a hydrogen-powered aircraft. ... For us, on the engine side, whether you're burning Jet A or whether you're burning hydrogen, it's not that different a technical problem.
finding: RTX saw hydrogen aircraft as a 2035-ish, 15-year horizon and considered it not very different technically for its engine business.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Now the GTF went a long way, right? There was a 16% better fuel burn, but 50% better on the emissions. Even that, we recognize we've got to do better. So we're going to invest in hydrogen.
finding: P&W pitched the GTF's 16% fuel burn gain but said it had to go further, committing to hydrogen investment (with defense money expected to come first).

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: From when you see 2019 levels of air traffic or passenger traffic recover, there will probably be a 6- to 9-month delay before we see our overall aftermarket business on the commercial side pick back up.
finding: RTX assumes the commercial engine aftermarket lags traffic recovery by 6-9 months.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: 2/3 of our business is defense-related, and those businesses remain strong with over $70 billion of backlog. That defense business also gives us the ability to continue to invest through this cycle and to make sure that we have the right technologies for the future.
finding: RTX uses its defense cash flow to fund continued commercial (including P&W) technology investment through the downturn.

doc: Baird Industrial Conference, Nov 2020 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Toby O'Brien, CFO (RTX)
quote: we announced the new Pratt facility in North Carolina. That's going to result in about $175 million in full annual run rate savings once we're up and running. And I think folks should think of that investment speaking to our confidence in the longer term
finding: P&W committed capital to a new airfoil plant during the COVID trough as a counter-cyclical investment, a signal of confidence in the long term.

doc: Cowen A&D Conference, Feb 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Toby O'Brien, CFO (RTX)
quote: on the commercial side, within OE, we're very well aligned with Boeing and Airbus production rates. So it comes down largely to aftermarket being the wildcard.
finding: P&W and Collins set OE output to follow airframer production schedules; the aftermarket is the swing factor in results.

speaker: Mike Dumais, Chief Transformation Officer (RTX)
quote: Obviously, it includes next-generation aircraft, where you're going to need very efficient engines and integrated systems. And some of these programs can have hundreds of billions of dollars of content.
finding: RTX sees next-generation aircraft programmes, which need very efficient engines, as prizes worth hundreds of billions of dollars of content.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: we're going to continue to invest in this business... These aren't guessing where the puck is going and making big bets. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks, mainly focused on structural cost reduction. Being a part of RTF enables us to continue to invest even in these tough times.
finding: P&W's stated investment stance in 2021 is disciplined and payback-driven, favouring cost reduction over big speculative bets, with RTX's balance sheet letting it keep investing through the downturn.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: It's making an investment in a new center line design, establishing a beachhead in a market in a leadership position and then continuing to spiral in technology... Over the last 10 years, Pratt Canada has certified over 25 engines across multiple segments. About 85% of those have been derivatives. So not a big centerline engine design investment, but derivatives.
finding: P&W's model is one new centreline core followed by many derivatives: 85% of P&WC's 25+ certifications in a decade were derivatives rather than new cores.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We've established a center of excellence, Carlsbad, California, to help develop the next-generation of CMC. North of that 2,400 degree Fahrenheit and, to Wes's point, a lighter material. This will enable us to both retrofit the existing fleet when it's ready. And then we can also, in the future, design around it
finding: P&W develops core technology (CMCs) to retrofit the existing fleet first and to design new engines around it later.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We see that as an opportunity in the short to medium range, general aviation, regional turboprop, helicopter segments... working with Collins and then working with governments in terms of funding these applications. There's a lot of demand out there. And there's a lot of governments who want a partner to make this happen.
finding: P&W pursues hybrid-electric propulsion in small segments first, with government co-funding.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: We think that can reduce emissions up to 80%. And we don't think it will cause us to have to do tremendous modifications to the engine... A lot of folks rightly so are out talking about the prospects and the potential of hydrogen. I think there's absolutely potential there. But that's a 2035 prospect.
finding: P&W favours sustainable aviation fuel as a near-term retrofit route needing few engine changes and places hydrogen at around 2035.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: When we get back to 2019 sales levels, we are not going back to 2019 headcount levels.
finding: P&W intends to keep COVID headcount cuts permanent and meet recovered volumes through productivity.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: These represent a $65 million investment with roughly 3 year paybacks. That'll allow capacity to increase by 80% and labor to decrease by 30%. We've got about 75 projects in the pipeline like this one. Things that are manageable investments with paybacks in that 2 to 3-year range
finding: P&W funds automation projects with 2-3 year paybacks, a short-payback hurdle for capital spending.

speaker: Chris Calio, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: we're going to be disciplined about E&D, CapEx and adding G&A. Each one of those will decrease as a percentage of sales during this plan period.
finding: P&W planned to shrink E&D and capex as a share of sales through 2025, i.e. no new large development programme in the plan.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: We have a very disciplined process here at RTX... to make sure they're aligned with our strategy, they're aligned with our customers and they have the right paybacks, and they generate the right returns... They come up through me, through Greg, up to our Board, depending on the various sizes.
finding: Engine investments at RTX need strategic fit, customer alignment and adequate paybacks and returns, with approvals escalating to the CEO and Board by size.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: what we really want to do is be platform-agnostic and have these technology insertions and be able to capitalize on retrofits and upgrades and things that keep the fleet flying
finding: RTX prefers platform-agnostic technology insertions, retrofits and upgrades to depending on new platform launches.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: we keep the brand identities of Pratt & Whitney and Collins Aerospace separate, so that when Chris or Steve goes to Beijing or Shanghai to visit AVIC or COMAC, they're coming as Collins Aerospace or Pratt & Whitney... the Chinese commercial aerospace market is the fastest-growing in the world. And we have to play there.
finding: RTX keeps P&W's brand separate from its defence identity so it can keep selling to COMAC and AVIC, China being the fastest-growing market.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: We are estimating slightly higher retirements over the period than we were before the pandemic. The good news is the GTF power and aircraft are flying quite a bit even through the pandemic. And so we think that the GTF is the architecture of the future, and we'll be expecting to ship many more of those over the coming years.
finding: P&W expects older aircraft to retire faster and be replaced by GTF-powered aircraft, which it calls the architecture of the future.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: it could get a little higher, not much. So I think that is about where we would peak out... I always like to think about negative engine margin as an investment. Now it goes through the P&L. But each aircraft that we put out there, it's positive NPV. It's got a highly assured aftermarket stream.
finding: P&W treats OE losses as an NPV-positive investment secured by the aftermarket; it expected the peak to be slightly above the roughly $1.2B a year of 2018-19 and rising with volume.

speaker: Neil Mitchill, CFO (RTX)
quote: we do continue to see some upward pressure on negative engine margin as the volumes increase but we do see that as a positive sign, frankly. Those are investments we're making in the future aftermarket. I'm not going to get into quantifying that today.
finding: P&W treats rising OE losses as an investment in the future aftermarket and welcomes higher volumes despite the margin hit, while declining to quantify them.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: the air traffic is going to grow 4% or 5% a year... We're positioned on both, obviously, a little bit different content on the A320 with the neo engines... there's plenty of time between now and then to get ready, if the ramp actually occurs as quickly as what Airbus hopes.
finding: RTX hedges across both narrowbodies (more content on the A320neo through the GTF) and will add capacity only once Airbus's ramp is confirmed.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: it is a shared platform between CFM and Pratt & Whitney... our goal here is to make sure that we have the most profitable piece of that business... we're not going to chase every last engine campaign... we want to be disciplined on pricing... Maybe it won't be 50%, maybe it will be 45%, maybe it will be 40%.
finding: On a platform shared with CFM, P&W says it prices for profit rather than volume and will accept a 40-50% share rather than chase every campaign.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: All I would tell you is, we remain in lockstep in terms of what's going on over the next 18 to 24 months with both Boeing and Airbus on the narrow-body. And we're certainly able to meet those demands today, and we'll work with them. If the demand is there, we will find a way to meet it.
finding: P&W plans capacity about 18-24 months ahead with the airframers and commits to follow real demand rather than lead with speculative capacity.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: We like our position both with Airbus and Boeing because we're on all those platforms in different capacities... It's really, in our mind, a supply chain issue. We are capacitized at the Airbus... level to be in the, call it, rate 63 range.
finding: P&W's GTF capacity was sized for an Airbus rate of about 63, below Airbus's rate-75 ambition, and RTX saw the supply chain rather than demand as the limit.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: It's the entire supply chain that we have to be cognizant of ramping up to those kinds of rates... to make sure that whatever rates we end up at are truly deliverable and frankly, sustainable for a period of time to make those investments make sense.
finding: P&W will only invest in more capacity if the higher airframer rates are sustained long enough to pay back the investment, so it does not follow aspirational rate targets automatically.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: My view is that negative engine margin is an investment. It happens to be one that we expense, but every time we sell an engine, we're securing a 20-, 25-year aftermarket stream. So I'm comfortable with the fact that we sell these engines at a loss. That's the business model that we're in today.
finding: P&W deliberately sells new engines at a loss as an investment in a 20-25 year aftermarket annuity, and judges the whole engine lifecycle as NPV positive.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: We participate in the used serviceable parts market ourselves to help with that, if you will... So we're constantly engaging with customers to address trade-offs between the maintenance cost and the operating cost. And it's our intention to do that here with the V.

finding: RTX complied with Russia sanctions immediately, writing off $1.3bn of roughly 10-year backlog and taking impairments at P&W and Collins in Q1 2022.
trigger: Russia invasion of Ukraine and sanctions, Feb 2022
response: reversed backlog, impairments, exited Russia JV

quote: The GTF aftermarket network expanded to 18 facilities worldwide, increasing PW1100G-JM shop visit output by approximately 30% year over year in 2024.

trigger: Powder metal fleet plan requiring incremental shop visits and elevated A320neo AOG
response: expanded GTF MRO network and shop visit throughput

quote: On October 16, 2017, Bombardier and Airbus announced an agreement to become partners on the CSeries aircraft program. We will continue to monitor the progress of the program and our ability to recover our investments, which we believe would be strengthened by this partnership.
finding: P&W welcomed Airbus taking a stake in the GTF-exclusive CSeries, seeing an Airbus-backed programme as improving its chance of recovering its launch investment.
response: P&W says recovery of its PW1500G investments would be strengthened; continues monitoring

quote: Of note, UTC’s businesses following the expected separation transactions will be significantly more reliant on three customers, namely Airbus, Boeing and the U.S. Government. ... its ability to fund capital expenditures and investments, pay dividends and service debt may be diminished.
finding: UTC acknowledged that after the spin-offs its engine and systems businesses would depend heavily on Airbus, Boeing and the U.S. Government, with less diversified cash to fund investment.

quote: Sales to Airbus (Pratt & Whitney’s largest customer by sales) were 31 percent and 36 percent of total Pratt & Whitney segm ent sales in 2019 and 2018, respectively, before taking into account discounts or financial incentives offered to customers. Sales to the U.S. Government were approximately 27 percent and 23 percent
finding: In 2019 P&W depended on Airbus for 31% and on the US government for 27% of segment sales. Its A320neo commercial exposure is balanced by military (F135) revenue.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s largest customer by sales is Airbus, with sales, prior to discounts and incentives, of 30%, 31% and 36% of total Pratt & Whitney segment sales in 2020, 2019 and 2018, respectively.
finding: Airbus's share of P&W sales fell from 36% in 2018 to about 30% in 2019-2020, but it remained P&W's dominant customer through the A320neo GTF.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s largest commercial customer by sales is Airbus, with sales, prior to discounts and incentives, of 31%, 30% and 31% of total Pratt & Whitney segment sales in 2021, 2020 and 2019, respectively.
finding: P&W is structurally dependent on Airbus: about 30% of segment sales every year from 2019 to 2021, so Airbus narrowbody decisions drive P&W's commercial fate.

quote: In certain limited circumstances, we pay deposits on behalf of our airline customers to secure production slots with the airframers, and such pre-delivery payments are included in our notes receivables.
finding: To win or keep engine business, RTX will fund airline pre-delivery deposits to the airframers, financing its customers' slots at Airbus or Boeing.

quote: Sales to Airbus primarily relate to Pratt & Whitney and Collins Aerospace products, and prior to discounts and incentives were approximately 12 %, 13 % and 22 % of total net sales in 2021, 2020 and 2019, respectively.
finding: Airbus was a fifth of UTC's sales in 2019; after the Raytheon merger it is 12-13% of RTX, so Airbus weighs less at group level while still dominating P&W's commercial book.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s largest commercial customer by sales is Airbus, with sales, prior to discounts and incentives, of 33%, 31% and 30% of total Pratt & Whitney segment sales in 2022, 2021 and 2020, respectively.
finding: Before the powder-metal year, Airbus was steadily about one third of P&W segment sales (30-33% in 2020-2022).

quote: our Contract liabilities include advance payments, in immaterial amounts, received from Russian customers on contracts we are currently unable to perform on due to global sanctions on Russia and export controls.
finding: After sanctions, P&W and Collins stopped performing on Russian customer contracts and held small advance payments that might have to be refunded.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s largest commercial customer by sales is Airbus, with sales, prior to discounts and incentives, of 48%, 33%, and 31% of total Pratt & Whitney segment sales in 2023, 2022, and 2021, respectively.
finding: P&W's dependence on Airbus deepened sharply by 2023 (48% of segment sales versus about 31-33% before), so the A320neo/GTF relationship dominates P&W's commercial fate.

quote: In 2023, Pratt & Whitney announced it will supply two GTF engines to power the Boeing X-66A sustainable flight demonstrator aircraft.
finding: P&W put the GTF on Boeing's X-66A sustainable flight demonstrator in 2023, a technology foothold with Boeing as well as Airbus.

quote: because we have significant business with Airbus and Boeing, our aerospace businesses could be adversely affected by challenges faced by these or other individual customers.
finding: RTX treats concentration on Airbus and Boeing as a material risk: airframer problems pass straight through to P&W and Collins.

quote: In certain limited circumstances, we pay deposits on behalf of our airline customers to secure production slots with the airframers
finding: RTX sometimes pays airframer pre-delivery deposits on behalf of airline customers to secure their production slots, a form of customer financing support.

quote: Aircraft financing commitments, in the form of debt or lease financing, are provided to certain commercial aerospace customers. The extent to which the financing commitments will be utilized is not currently known, since customers may be able to obtain more favorable terms from other financing sources.
finding: RTX offers airlines backstop aircraft financing as part of engine campaigns, which customers draw only when they cannot find better terms elsewhere.

quote: The largest contributor to our Commercial aerospace and other commercial sales is Airbus. Sales to Airbus primarily relate to Pratt & Whitney and Collins products, and prior to discounts and incentives were approximately 17 %, 14 %, and 12 % of total net sales in 2023, 2022, and 2021, respectively.
finding: Airbus grew to about 17% of total RTX sales by 2023, mainly through P&W and Collins, making Airbus RTX's largest commercial customer.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s largest commercial customer by sales is Airbus, with sales, prior to discounts and incentives, of 31%, 48%, and 33% of total Pratt & Whitney segment sales in 2024, 2023, and 2022, respectively.
finding: Airbus's share of P&W sales fell back to 31% in 2024 from the 48% outlier of 2023, returning to the long-run one-third dependence.

quote: Revenue passenger miles (RPMs), available seat miles, and the general economic health of airline carriers and airframers, as well as the financial strength and performance of airframers, are key barometers for our commercial aerospace operations.
finding: In the FY2024 filing RTX added airframers' financial strength and performance to its key commercial barometers, showing heightened sensitivity to airframer health.

quote: Sales to Airbus primarily relate to Pratt & Whitney and Collins products, and prior to discounts and incentives were approximately 14 %, 17 %, and 14 % of total net sales in 2024, 2023, and 2022, respectively.
finding: Airbus remained RTX's largest commercial customer at about 14% of total sales in 2024.

quote: Our financing predominantly relates to leased engines, often provided through the customers’ aftermarket maintenance coverage, and to a lesser extent, notes and lease receivables.
finding: RTX's customer financing is mostly leased engines provided through customers' maintenance coverage, i.e. spare-engine support tied to service agreements.

quote: changes in production volumes of one or more of our significant customers as a result of business, labor, or other challenges, and the resulting effect on its or their demand for our products and services;
finding: New in the FY2024 filing: RTX lists a significant customer's production cuts from business or labour problems as a risk to its demand.

quote: In 2016, we increased our collaboration intangible assets by approximately $388 million, of which $345 million represented payments made under our 2012 agreement to acquire Rolls-Royce's ownership and collaboration interests in IAE.
finding: P&W is still paying Rolls-Royce for the 2012 IAE buy-out, at about $345m in 2016, showing it paid over time to consolidate the V2500 franchise.

quote: In connection with our 2012 agreement to acquire Rolls-Royce's ownership and collaboration interests in IAE, additional payments are due to Rolls-Royce contingent upon each hour flown through June 2027 by the V2500-powered aircraft in service
finding: The IAE buy-out price is partly contingent on V2500 flight hours through June 2027, so P&W pays RR out of the aftermarket stream it acquired.

finding: P&W's backlog grew about $9bn in 2016 on GTF orders, but it admits some contracts in it may cost more than they bring in.

quote: In accordance with our revenue recognition policy, losses, if any, on long-term contracts are provided for when anticipated. There were no material loss provisions recorded on OEM contracts in continuing operations in 2016 or 2015.
finding: Despite negative engine margins, P&W booked no material OEM loss provisions in 2015-16, consistent with GTF campaigns being judged profitable including the aftermarket.

quote: Capital expenditures increased from 2012 through 2016 as we expanded capacity to meet expected demand within our aerospace businesses for the next generation engine platforms.
finding: UTC raised capex every year from 2012 to 2016 ($1.3bn to $1.7bn) to build capacity for next-generation engines, the GTF above all.

quote: Proceeds from the sale were used to fund $6 billion of share repurchases through accelerated share repurchase (ASR) agreements entered into on November 11, 2015.
finding: UTC returned the Sikorsky sale proceeds to shareholders through a $6bn accelerated buyback, showing a strong shareholder-return priority alongside P&W investment.

quote: Quarterly cash dividends and share repurchases under our share repurchase program constitute components of our capital allocation strategy, which we fund with free operating cash flow, borrowings and divestitures.
finding: UTC funds dividends and buybacks from free cash flow, borrowing and divestitures, so engine investment competes with shareholder returns.

quote: The organic increase in total cost of products and services sold of 3% in 2015 is attributable to the organic sales increase noted above and the unfavorable OEM sales mix and the related losses on OEM engine shipments, within Pratt & Whitney.
finding: Shipping more new engines raised P&W's costs because each OEM engine shipment carries a loss.

quote: lower gross margin at Pratt & Whitney (60 basis points) driven by unfavorable year-over-year contract performance and contract termination benefits and settlements, and an increase in negative engine margin
finding: In the GTF entry-into-service year, a rising negative engine margin at P&W cut 60bp from UTC's consolidated gross margin.

quote: The majority of the company-funded spending is incurred by the aerospace businesses and relates largely to the next generation engine product family at Pratt & Whitney ... higher research and development costs within Pratt & Whitney (2%) as development programs progress towards certification
finding: Most of UTC's $2.3bn company-funded R&D went to the GTF family, and it rose in 2016 as more GTF variants moved toward certification.

quote: The year-over-year decrease in company-funded research and development (8%) in 2015, compared with 2014, reflects lower research and development within Pratt & Whitney (5%) primarily related to lower development costs of multiple Geared TurboFan platforms as development is completed and certain of these engines enter into service
finding: P&W's own R&D falls as each GTF variant certifies, so development spending peaks before entry into service and then tapers.
P&W segment margin fell from 13.8% (2014) to 6.1% (2015) and recovered to 10.4% (2016) as GTF entry into service began.

quote: lower large commercial engine profit contribution (8%) primarily driven by higher negative engine margin ... These decreases were partially offset by: ... profit contribution from strong commercial aftermarket volume (33%)
finding: In 2016 aftermarket volume was P&W's main profit driver, more than offsetting a deeper negative margin on new large commercial engines.

quote: The organic sales increase of 6% primarily reflects higher commercial aftermarket sales (8%), and higher military engine and aftermarket sales (2%), partially offset by unfavorable year-over-year contract performance, contract termination benefits and contract settlements (2%) and lower commercial engine sales volume (1%).
finding: P&W's 2016 growth came from the aftermarket, not new engine sales, during the V2500-to-GTF transition.

quote: The operational profit decrease (12%) was due to: ... higher negative engine margin within the Large Commercial Engine business and lower volume within P&WC (15%)
finding: In 2015, before GTF entry into service, higher negative engine margin was already the largest drag on P&W's operating profit.

finding: P&W expected its deferred early-GTF excess unit costs to keep growing through 2017, showing that the ramp's learning-curve losses were still building.

quote: We expect 2017 investments in customer financing assets to increase by approximately $400 million, primarily due to increased levels of investment in commercial aircraft engines and products under lease.
finding: P&W uses its balance sheet to lease engines to customers, and expected to add about $400m of such financing in 2017.

quote: At December 31, 2016, we had commercial aerospace financing and other contractual commitments of approximately $14.4 billion related to commercial aircraft and certain contractual rights to provide product on new aircraft platforms, of which as much as $1.3 billion may be required to be disbursed during 2017. ... our collaborators' share of these commitments was approximately $4.6 billion
finding: UTC carries large financing and platform-access commitments to customers, about a third of which P&W's collaboration partners share.

finding: UTC's rising capex went mainly into new programmes and new facilities at P&W.
P&W's segment assets grew about $4.8bn over 2014-16 while its own capex stayed around $0.7bn a year and D&A rose, reflecting the GTF build-up.

finding: P&W treats GTF teething problems as normal for a new engine: it fixed them with modifications and paid through warranty provisions, customer settlements and lower contract margins, so P&W carries the cost of early-life durability issues.
