finding: By end-2021 the GTF installed base was over 1,100 aircraft at 58 airlines on three platforms, while the legacy V2500 fleet (250 million flight hours) remained a large aftermarket annuity.

quote: a significant prolonged increase in inflation could negatively impact the cost of materials and components, particularly with respect to our commercial business operations within Collins Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney.
finding: RTX flagged in the FY2021 filing that P&W's commercial business is especially exposed to input-cost inflation, which it may not be able to pass through on long-term contracts.

quote: The level of orders received for the Geared Turbofan family of engines, coupled with a requirement to achieve mature production levels in a very short time frame, require significant additional manufacturing and supply chain capacity. ... if we identify or experience issues with in-service engines, we may not meet customers’ delivery schedules
finding: Even in FY2021, after COVID, RTX still named the GTF ramp to mature production in a very short time as its key technology risk, with supplier performance and in-service engine issues threatening delivery schedules and liquidated damages - a persistent theme.

quote: Turkish companies supply us with components, some of which are sole-sourced, primarily in our aerospace operations for commercial and military engines and aerospace products.
finding: P&W's engine supply chain includes sole-sourced Turkish suppliers, a concentration risk it accepted for cost reasons.

quote: While the investigation has focused on alleged hiring restrictions between and among Pratt & Whitney and certain of its suppliers of outsourced engineering services ... On December 15, 2021, a criminal indictment was filed ... against a former Pratt & Whitney employee and other employees of certain outsourced engineering suppliers
finding: P&W relies on outsourced engineering suppliers. In 2021 a DOJ antitrust probe into alleged hiring restrictions between P&W and those suppliers led to the indictment of a former P&W employee, a sign of how tight engineering labour was.

quote: The GTF family now powers more than 1,400 aircraft across 64 airlines and three aircraft platforms: Airbus A320neo family, Airbus A220 and Embraer E-Jets E2.
finding: The GTF installed base grew to over 1,400 aircraft at 64 airlines by end-2022 (from about 1,100 at end-2021).

quote: coupled with a requirement to achieve mature production levels in a very short time frame, require significant additional manufacturing and supply chain capacity. If any of our production ramp-up efforts are delayed... and/or if we identify or experience issues with in-service engines, we may not meet customers’ delivery schedules
finding: Before the powder-metal disclosure, P&W's main stated GTF risk was the delivery ramp, and it already named in-service engine issues as a threat to customer schedules.

quote: which could result in material additional costs, including liquidated damages or other liabilities that could be assessed under existing contracts.
finding: P&W's existing GTF contracts include liquidated damages for late deliveries, so ramp slippage costs it money directly.

quote: We work continuously to mitigate the effects of these supply chain issues and risks, including providing raw materials and technical support to our suppliers and subcontractors, as well as providing them with access to our contract labor networks to augment supplier and subcontractor workforces; seeking alternate supply sources; increasing our inventory of available materials and parts
finding: RTX responded to 2022 supply shortages by supporting suppliers directly (materials, technical help, labour), second-sourcing and building inventory.
response: supplier support, alternate sources, more inventory

quote: In addition, as the ongoing recovery in commercial air travel continues, the anticipated increase in new aircraft deliveries and increased demand for our products and services will add to these supply chain and labor market challenges.
finding: RTX expected rising airframer delivery rates in the recovery to add strain on an already stretched engine supply chain.

quote: The GTF family now powers more than 1,700 aircraft for 70 operators across three aircraft platforms: Airbus A320neo family, Airbus A220, and Embraer E-Jets E2.
finding: By end-2023 the GTF installed base exceeded 1,700 aircraft at 70 operators on three platforms, up from about 1,100 aircraft at end-2021.

quote: The level of orders received for the Geared Turbofan family of engines, coupled with a requirement to achieve mature production levels in a very short time frame, require significant manufacturing and supply chain capacity.
finding: P&W acknowledges that the GTF's order book forced it to reach mature production rates very quickly, straining manufacturing and supply chain capacity.

quote: If any of our production or maintenance, repair, and overhaul ramp-up efforts are delayed, if suppliers cannot timely deliver or perform to our standards, if any other engine models are found to be materially impacted by the powder metal issue... we may not meet customer requirements, which could result in material additional costs, including liquidated damages or other liabilities.
finding: P&W's GTF commitments to customers carry liquidated damages if its production and MRO ramp slips, so execution failures translate directly into customer payments.

quote: This determination and corresponding fleet actions have significantly increased both the incremental number of PW1100 GTF engines that will need to be removed and the incremental number of shop visits necessary to perform the inspections as compared to estimates prior to this determination. Actual and future estimated aircraft on ground levels for the A320neo family of aircraft have therefore increased.
finding: The 2023 powder-metal finding forced many more PW1100 GTF removals and shop visits than planned, grounding more A320neo aircraft.

quote: As a result, we have and will continue to incur significant customer support and mitigation costs and significant labor, material, and related costs. This matter has caused reputational harm and has negatively impacted, and will continue to impact, our results of operations and financial condition.
finding: RTX admits the powder-metal crisis caused reputational harm and ongoing customer support, mitigation and labor/material costs, which P&W carries.

quote: In addition, other engine models within Pratt & Whitney’s fleet contain parts manufactured with affected powder metal. The negative impacts to our company arising from the Powder Metal matter could increase if any other engine models are found to be materially impacted by this rare condition.
finding: The powder-metal exposure extends beyond the PW1100 to other P&W engine models, leaving open further installed-base costs.

quote: As a result of these procurement issues, the production flow in our factories has been negatively impacted, which has, in turn, hindered our ability to perform on our commitments to customers and negatively affected our results of operations, financial condition, and liquidity.
finding: In 2023 supply chain shortages disrupted RTX factory flow and hindered delivery on customer commitments.

quote: On August 4, 2023, Pratt & Whitney issued a special instruction (SI), to operators of PW1100 GTF powered A320neo aircraft, which required accelerated inspections and engine removals covering an initial subset of operational engines, no later than September 15, 2023.
finding: P&W acted through its safety management system with a fleet instruction in August 2023 forcing early removals of a first subset of GTF engines within six weeks.

quote: This updated plan requires a combination of part inspections and retirements for some high pressure turbine and high pressure compressor parts... the actions are expected to result in significant incremental shop visits through the end of 2026. As a result, Pratt & Whitney expects a significant increase in aircraft on ground levels for the PW1100 powered A320neo fleet through 2026.
finding: P&W's GTF fleet plan retires affected HPT and HPC parts and implies extra shop visits and elevated A320neo groundings through 2026.

quote: Other engine models within Pratt & Whitney’s fleet contain parts manufactured with affected powder metal, and while Pratt & Whitney continues to evaluate the impact of this powder metal issue on other engine models within its fleet, we do not currently believe there will be any significant financial impact with respect to these other engine models.
finding: P&W took the position at end-2023 that the powder-metal issue on other engine models would not have a significant financial impact.

quote: On November 7, 2023 and January 30, 2024, the Company received subpoenas from the SEC seeking engineering, operational, organizational, accounting, and financial documents in connection with an investigation relating to the Company’s disclosures in 2023 of issues arising from Pratt & Whitney’s use of powder metal
finding: The GTF crisis spread into securities class actions and an SEC investigation of RTX's powder-metal disclosures, adding legal and governance costs.

quote: The GTF family now powers more than 2,200 aircraft for 85 operators across three aircraft platforms: Airbus A320neo family, Airbus A220, and Embraer E-Jets E2. In 2024, Pratt & Whitney received FAA certification for the GTF engine that will power the Airbus A321XLR aircraft.
finding: Despite the groundings, the GTF fleet kept growing (over 2,200 aircraft, 85 operators by end-2024) and P&W certified the GTF for Airbus's A321XLR.

quote: and/or if we identify or experience other issues, including durability issues, with in-service engines in the GTF family of engines (or other engines), whether for manufacturing reasons or otherwise, we may not meet customer requirements, which could result in material additional costs, including liquidated damages or other liabilities.
finding: By FY2024 P&W explicitly lists GTF durability issues, beyond powder metal, as a risk that could trigger liquidated damages and other liabilities.

quote: The level of orders received for the GTF family of engines, coupled with a requirement to achieve mature production levels in a very short time frame, have required significant growth in our manufacturing and supply chain capacity.
finding: By 2024 RTX described the GTF ramp as having already required significant capacity growth, the persistent cost of a large order book.

quote: This determination and corresponding fleet actions have resulted in, and are expected to continue to result in, an elevated level of aircraft on ground for the A320neo family of aircraft and significant incremental shop visits necessary to perform inspections on PW1100 GTF engines through the end of 2026.
finding: A year and a half after the disclosure, P&W still expected A320neo groundings and extra GTF shop visits to continue through end-2026.

quote: Guidance to affected operators was released via service bulletins (SB) and SI in November 2023, and this guidance has been reflected in airworthiness directives issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Consistent with previous information, the actions are resulting in significant incremental shop visits.
finding: P&W's self-initiated GTF fleet plan was adopted into FAA airworthiness directives, and it was producing significant extra shop visits in 2024.

quote: Other engine models within Pratt & Whitney’s fleet contain parts manufactured with affected powder metal, but we do not currently believe there will be any resultant significant financial impact with respect to these other engine models at this time.
finding: P&W kept its position through 2024 that the powder-metal issue would not have a significant financial impact on other engine models.

quote: Furthermore, our competitors, including our customers, may develop competing technologies which gain market acceptance in advance of or instead of our products. ... the possibility exists that competitors or customers will develop aftermarket services and aftermarket parts for our products which attract customers and adversely impact our return on investment on new products.
finding: Already in 2019, P&W named its customers (airframers and airlines) as potential aftermarket competitors that could erode the return on a new engine.

quote: Moreover, we have seen highly competitive pricing, in which a bidder may anticipate making a substantial investment in a program in order to win the work. ... Highly competitive activity within the commercial aerospace industry has included substantial discounts and other financial incentives
finding: RTX reports that bidders, rivals included, invest heavily up front to win programmes. Engine competitions are bought positions, which sets the bar for P&W's own terms.

quote: Highly competitive activity within the commercial aerospace industry has included substantial discounts and other financial incentives, performance and operating cost guarantees, and participation in financing arrangements, in order to secure both new engine business and the aftermarket revenues associated with these products.
finding: RTX describes engine competitions as won with deep discounts, guarantees and financing to capture aftermarket revenue - the industry norm P&W plays by when bidding for new platforms.

quote: the possibility exists that competitors or customers will develop aftermarket services and aftermarket parts for our products that attract customers and adversely impact our return on investment on new products.
finding: P&W's return on a new engine depends on capturing its aftermarket; RTX sees third-party and customer-developed parts and services (including by airframers) as a direct threat to that return.

quote: In view of the risks and costs associated with developing new engines, Pratt & Whitney has entered into collaboration arrangements in which sales, costs and risks are shared. At December 31, 2016, the interests of third party participants in Pratt & Whitney-directed commercial jet engine programs ranged from 14% to 50%. ... continues to pursue additional collaboration partners.
finding: P&W does not fund new commercial engines alone: it lays off 14-50% of each programme's sales, costs and risks on risk-sharing partners and keeps seeking more partners.

quote: Pratt & Whitney is the principal participant in all existing collaborative arrangements. There are no individually significant collaborative arrangements and none of the collaborators exceed a 31% share in an individual program.
finding: P&W shares risk but keeps programme control: it leads every collaboration and no single partner holds more than 31% of any programme.

quote: Pratt & Whitney holds a 61% net program share interest in the IAE International Aero Engines AG (IAE) collaboration with MTU and JAEC and a 49.5% ownership interest in IAE. Additionally, Pratt & Whitney holds a 59% net program interest in the International Aero Engines, LLC (IAE LLC) collaboration, and a 59% ownership interest in IAE LLC.
finding: P&W sells both its A320-family engines (V2500 and the GTF PW1100G-JM) through IAE partnerships with MTU and JAEC, keeping about 60% of the programme economics.

quote: Pratt & Whitney has interests in other engine programs, including a 50 percent ownership interest in the Engine Alliance (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation, which markets and manufactures the GP7000 engine for the Airbus A380 aircraft. Pratt & Whitney has entered into risk and revenue sharing arrangements with third parties for 40 percent of the products and services
finding: P&W will enter a 50/50 joint venture with a direct rival (GE) for a widebody engine and then lay off 40% of its own share to risk-sharing partners.

quote: Pratt & Whitney has developed the PurePower® PW1000G Geared TurboFan engine which entered into service in January 2016 and is intended to enable it to power both currently-proposed and future aircraft.
finding: P&W treats the GTF as a scalable engine family to be offered on future aircraft as well as current ones.

quote: The success of these aircraft and the PurePower® family of engines is dependent upon many factors including technological accomplishments, program execution, aircraft demand, and regulatory approval. Based on these factors, as well as the level of success of aircraft program launches by aircraft manufacturers and other conditions, additional investment in the PurePower® program may be required.
finding: P&W says its GTF investment depends on airframers' launch success and warns that more investment may be required.

quote: In particular, Pratt & Whitney experiences intense competition for new commercial airframe/engine combinations. Engine suppliers may offer substantial discounts and other financial incentives, performance and operating cost guarantees, and participation in financing arrangements, in an effort to compete for the aftermarket associated with these engines.
finding: P&W competes for new engine positions by discounting and by offering incentives, guarantees and financing, because the prize is the aftermarket.

quote: These OEM engine sales may result in losses on the engine sales, which ... economically are recovered through the sales and profits generated over the engine's maintenance cycle.
finding: P&W knowingly sells new engines at a loss and relies on the maintenance cycle to recover it.

quote: In the large commercial engine and wheels and brakes businesses, when the combined original equipment and aftermarket arrangements for each individual sales campaign are profitable, we record original equipment product losses, as applicable, at the time of delivery.
finding: P&W judges each engine sales campaign on OE plus aftermarket together and accepts OE losses so long as the combined campaign is profitable.

quote: the possibility exists that competitors will develop aftermarket services and aftermarket parts for our products which attract customers and adversely impact our return on investment on new products.
finding: P&W sees third-party aftermarket competition as a direct threat to the return on its new engines, which rests on capturing the aftermarket.

quote: We continue to invest in new platforms and new markets to position the Company for long-term growth, while remaining focused on innovation for growth, structural cost reduction, disciplined capital allocation and the execution of customer and shareowner commitments.
finding: UTC presents investment in new platforms as balanced against cost reduction, disciplined capital allocation and shareholder commitments.

quote: FMPs are comprehensive long-term spare part and maintenance agreements with our customers. We expect a continued shift to FMPs in lieu of transactional spare part sales as new engines enter customers' fleets on FMP and legacy fleets are retired.
finding: P&W expects new engines such as the GTF to go into fleets on long-term fleet management contracts instead of time-and-materials spares, so aftermarket value is locked in when the engine is sold.

quote: Also included within other intangible assets are payments made to secure certain contractual rights to provide product on new commercial aerospace platforms. ... The gross value of these contractual commitments at December 31, 2016 was approximately $10.8 billion, of which approximately $2.0 billion has been paid to date.
finding: UTC pays airframers to secure positions on new platforms, with about $10.8bn committed, so buying platform access is part of how it wins engine and systems positions.

quote: The recoverability of these intangibles is dependent upon the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms including the associated aftermarket revenue streams.
finding: UTC ties the value of what it pays for platform access to the aircraft's success and its aftermarket revenue, making a platform bet an aftermarket bet.

quote: In our aerospace businesses, we may make participation payments to certain customers to secure certain contractual rights. To the extent these rights are incremental and are supported by the incremental cash flows obtained, they are capitalized as intangible assets.
finding: UTC pays customers participation payments to win positions and capitalises them only when incremental cash flows support them, an explicit return test.

quote: We extend performance and operating cost guarantees beyond our normal service and warranty policies for extended periods on some of our products, particularly commercial aircraft engines. Liability under such guarantees is based upon future product performance and durability.
finding: P&W sells engines with long-term performance and operating-cost guarantees, so it carries durability risk after the sale.

quote: To generate an acceptable return on our investment in these contracts, we must be able to accurately estimate our costs ... Some of our contracts provide for liquidated damages in the event that we are unable to perform and deliver in accordance with the contractual specifications and schedule.
finding: UTC prices bids to earn an acceptable return on estimated cost and accepts liquidated-damages exposure if it misses specification or schedule.

quote: We expect a continued shift to FMPs in lieu of transactional spare part sales as new engines enter customers' fleets on FMP and legacy fleets are retired. In 2017, as compared with 2016, total commercial aerospace aftermarket sales increased 11% at Pratt & Whitney
finding: P&W kept steering new-engine customers onto long-term fleet management contracts while its legacy-fleet aftermarket grew 11%, continuing its 2016 approach.

quote: Furthermore, because of the lengthy research and development cycle involved in bringing products in these business segments to market, we cannot predict the economic conditions that will exist when any new product is complete.
finding: UTC acknowledges that new engine programmes are committed years before the market they will be sold into is known.

quote: Pratt & Whitney is the principal participant in all existing collaborative arrangements, with the exception of the Engine Alliance (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation, which markets and manufactures the GP7000 engine for the Airbus A380 aircraft. There are no individually significant collaborative arrangements and none of the collaborators exceed a 31% share in an individual program.
finding: P&W leads all its collaborations except the 50/50 Engine Alliance with GE, the one case where it shares control with a rival.

quote: The gross value of these contractual commitments at December 31, 2017 was approximately $10.6 billion , of which approximately $2.3 billion has been paid to date. ... The recoverability of these intangibles is dependent upon the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms including the associated aftermarket revenue streams.
finding: UTC kept paying for platform positions ($2.3bn paid of $10.6bn committed) and still tied their value to each platform's aftermarket, continuing the 2016 practice.

quote: On November 26, 2018, the Company announced its intention to separate into three independent companies: (1) UTC, an aerospace company comprised of the Collins Aerospace Systems and Pratt & Whitney businesses, (2) Otis, and (3) Carrier.
finding: In late 2018 UTC chose to become a pure aerospace company, spinning off Otis and Carrier, so P&W would sit in an aerospace-only parent without the building businesses' cash flows.

quote: United Technologies, comprised of Collins Aerospace Systems and Pratt & Whitney, will be the preeminent systems supplier to the aerospace and defense industry;
finding: After the separation UTC planned to position P&W alongside Collins as part of an integrated aerospace systems supplier, not a stand-alone engine maker.

quote: the interests of third-party participants in Pratt & Whitney-directed commercial jet engine programs ranged from approximately 13 percent to 50 percent. ... risk and revenue sharing arrangements with third parties for 40 percent of the products and 25 percent of the services that Pratt & Whitney is responsible for providing to the EA.
finding: P&W kept its risk-sharing model in 2018 (partners 13-50% per programme) and disclosed that on the GE joint venture it lays off 40% of products but only 25% of services, keeping more of the aftermarket.

quote: These OEM engine sales may result in losses on the engine sales, which economically are recovered through the sales and profits generated over the engine's maintenance cycle. ... There were no material loss provisions recorded on OEM contracts in continuing operations in 2018 or 2017.
finding: Through the GTF ramp P&W kept its razor-and-blade logic unchanged and booked no OEM loss provisions in 2016-2018, still judging the campaigns profitable once aftermarket is included.

quote: The gross value of these contractual commitments at December 31, 2018 was approximately $11.3 billion, of which approximately $2.7 billion has been paid to date. ... The recoverability of these intangibles is dependent upon the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms including the associated aftermarket revenue streams.
finding: UTC's commitments to pay for platform positions rose to $11.3bn in 2018 ($2.7bn paid), so buying positions on airframes remained a standing practice.

quote: UTC holds a 61 percent program share interest in the IAE International Aero Engines AG (IAE) collaboration with MTU Aero Engines AG (MTU) and Japanese Aero Engines Corporation (JAEC). Pratt & Whitney also holds a 59 percent program share interest in the International Aero Engines, LLC (IAE LLC) collaboration with MTU and JAEC.
finding: In the FY2019 filing P&W ran both A320-family engines through partnerships it controls: 61% of the V2500 and 59% of the A320neo GTF, with MTU and JAEC as junior partners.

quote: a 50 percent ownership interest in Engine Alliance, LLC (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation, which sells and provides maintenance services for the GP7000 engine for the Airbus A380 aircraft ... Pratt & Whitney has entered into risk and revenue sharing arrangements with third parties for 40 percent of the products and 25 percent of the services
finding: P&W's widebody engine position was a 50/50 JV with rival GE on the A380 (GP7000), and it passed 40% of its product share and 25% of its service share to partners. It took widebody risk only in heavily shared form, and Airbus was ending the A380 after 2021.

quote: The success of these aircraft and engines is dependent upon many factors, including technological accomplishments, program execution, aircraft demand, and regulatory approval. As a result of these factors, as well as the level of success of aircraft program launches by aircraft manufacturers and other conditions, additional investment in these engine programs may be required.
finding: P&W acknowledges that its engine returns depend on how well airframers' programme launches go (it then had GTFs on the SpaceJet and MC-21), and that a weak launch can require it to invest more in the engine.

quote: At times, our aerospace businesses also enter into firm fixed-price or cost-share development contracts, which may require us to bear cost overruns related to unforeseen technical and design challenges that arise during the development and early production stages of the program.
finding: UTC accepts fixed-price or cost-share development deals, so P&W carries the development and early-production overrun risk on new engines.

quote: Of note, even if the combination with Raytheon is completed, UTC’s businesses following the expected separation transactions will be significantly more reliant on three customers, namely Airbus, Boeing and the U.S. Government.
finding: UTC chose to become a pure aerospace and defence company, knowingly concentrating the future RTX on three customers: Airbus, Boeing and the US government.

quote: The majority of the company-funded spending is incurred by the aerospace businesses and relates largely to the next generation engine product family at Pratt & Whitney and systems being developed to support new aircraft and other program introductions at Collins Aerospace Systems.
finding: Before COVID, most of UTC's company-funded R&D was spent in aerospace, mainly on P&W's next-generation engine family and on Collins systems for new aircraft. The engine family was a top call on group development money.

quote: Pratt & Whitney experiences intense competition for new commercial airframe/engine combinations. Engine suppliers may offer substantial discounts and other financial incentives ... These OEM engine sales may result in losses on the engine sales, which economically are recovered through the sales and profits generated over the engine's maintenance cycle.
finding: P&W's stated model is to sell engines at a loss, with discounts, guarantees and financing, to win airframe/engine positions, and to recover the loss over the engine's maintenance cycle.

quote: We expect a continued shift to long-term aftermarket service agreements in lieu of transactional spare part sales as new aerospace products enter our customers' fleets under long-term aftermarket service agreements and legacy fleets are retired. In 2019, as compared with 2018, total commercial aerospace aftermarket sales increased 2% at Pratt & Whitney
finding: UTC expected new engines to go into fleets under long-term service agreements rather than transactional spare-part sales, while legacy fleets retire. P&W's commercial aftermarket grew only 2% in 2019.

quote: which approximately $3.2 billion has been paid to date. We record these payments as intangible assets when such payment s are no longer conditional. The recoverability of these intangibles is dependent upon the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms including the associated aftermarket revenue streams.
finding: By end-2019 UTC had paid about $3.2bn for platform positions, with further payments conditional. The value of those positions depends on the airframer programme and its aftermarket.

quote: For new commitments, we generally record loss provisions at the earlier of contract announcement or contract signing ... In the commercial engine and wheels and brakes businesses, when the combined original equipment and aftermarket arrangement for each individual sales campaign are profitable, we record original equipment product losses, as applicable, at the time of delivery.
finding: P&W judges each engine sales campaign on combined OE plus aftermarket profitability. If the campaign is profitable it accepts OE losses and books them only at delivery. This is the same policy in FY2019 through FY2021.

quote: we offer customers certain incentives to purchase our products. These incentives may result in payments made to customers. In addition, we may make participation payments to certain aerospace customers to secure certain contractual rights. To the extent these rights are incremental and are supported by the incremental cash flows obtained, they are capitalized as intangible assets.
finding: UTC makes participation payments to aerospace customers to secure contractual rights and capitalises them when incremental cash flows support them. Paying customers for positions is a standard tool.

quote: We have long-term aftermarket maintenance contracts with commercial aerospace industry customers for which revenue is recognized over-time in proportion to actual costs incurred relative to total expected costs to be incurred over the respective contract periods. Billings, however, are typically based on factors such as aircraft or engine flight hours.
finding: P&W bills its long-term maintenance contracts mainly per aircraft or engine flight hour, so aftermarket cash moves with fleet utilisation.

quote: Our commercial aftermarket operations continue to evolve as a significant portion of our aerospace operations’ customers are covered under long-term aftermarket service agreements at both Collins Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney. These agreements are comprehensive long-term spare part and service agreements with our customers.
finding: P&W keeps moving its customers onto comprehensive long-term spares and service agreements to lock in the aftermarket.

quote: The gross value of these contractual commitments at December 31, 2020 was approximately $11.6 billion, of which approximately $3.3 billion has been paid to date. We regularly assess the recoverability of these intangibles, which is dependent upon our assumptions around the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms
finding: RTX had committed $11.6bn gross to buy platform positions by end-2020 and had paid only $3.3bn, so most of the cost of the positions it holds was still to be paid.

quote: Pratt & Whitney is the principal participant in all existing collaborative arrangements, with the exception of the Engine Alliance (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation ... none of the collaborators individually have more than a 31 % share in an individual program.
finding: In the FY2020 filing no single P&W collaborator held more than 31% of a programme (unchanged since FY2016). The cap fell to 25% in FY2021, so P&W kept control in every partnership except the equal JV with GE on the A380.

quote: In view of the risks and costs associated with developing new engines, Pratt & Whitney has entered into collaboration arrangements in which revenues, costs and risks are shared with third parties. At December 31, 2021, the interests of third-party collaboration participants in Pratt & Whitney-directed jet engine programs ranged, in the aggregate per program, from 13% to 49%.
finding: P&W persists in laying off 13-49% of each engine programme's revenues, costs and risks on partners rather than funding new engines alone, essentially unchanged from earlier years.

quote: Customer selections of aircraft engines, components and systems can also have a significant impact on future sales of parts and services. ... Some competitors may offer substantial discounts and other financial incentives, performance and operating cost guarantees, and participation in financing arrangements in an effort to compete for the aftermarket associated with these products.
finding: RTX frames engine selection as a contest for the downstream aftermarket, in which rivals buy positions with OE discounts, guarantees and financing - the razor/razor-blade logic that makes aggressive OE terms rational.

quote: because of the lengthy research and development cycle involved in bringing products in these business segments to market, we cannot predict the economic conditions that will exist when any new product is ready to enter into service.
finding: RTX acknowledges that a new engine is launched blind to the market conditions at entry into service, one reason it shares programme risk with partners and ties launches to firm demand.

quote: The evolving nature of these standards, along with the long duration of development, production and aftermarket support programs, creates uncertainty regarding program profitability, particularly with our aircraft engine products. Development efforts divert resources from other potential investments in our businesses
finding: RTX singles out aircraft engines as the products whose programme profitability is most uncertain because of their long development-to-aftermarket life, and treats engine development as competing with other uses of RTX capital.

quote: we anticipate that we will need to make additional investments in new technologies and capabilities ... Our competitors may develop these in-demand technologies before we do, their new technologies may be deemed by our customers to be superior to technologies we may develop
finding: By FY2021 RTX accepted that climate pressure would force added investment in lower-emission technologies and that rivals could get there first, a driver for next-generation engine spending.

quote: In 2021, 2020, and 2019 we increased our collaboration intangible assets by approximately $188 million, $172 million, $351 million, respectively, which primarily relates to payments made under our 2012 agreement to acquire Rolls-Royce’s collaboration interests in International Aero Engines AG (IAE).
finding: P&W keeps paying Rolls-Royce for the IAE/V2500 interest it bought in 2012 - about $170-350 million a year in 2019-21 - the price of consolidating the V2500 aftermarket.

quote: Also included within intangible assets are exclusivity assets, which are payments made to secure certain contractual rights to provide products on new commercial aerospace platforms. At December 31, 2021, our exclusivity assets, net of accumulated amortization, was approximately $2.4 billion, and our remaining estimated commitments, net of collaborator share, were approximately $8.9 billion.
finding: RTX pays to secure sole positions on new aircraft platforms: $2.4 billion was already capitalised and a further $8.9 billion was committed at end-2021. Winning a platform costs cash up front.

quote: We regularly assess the recoverability of these intangibles, which is dependent upon our assumptions around the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms including the associated aftermarket revenue streams, and the related future cash flows.
finding: Whether platform-access payments pay off depends on the aircraft programme's success and the aftermarket it generates, so P&W's value is tied to the airframer's programme.

quote: Exclusivity assets are commercial aerospace payments made to secure certain contractual rights to provide product on new aircraft platforms. We classify amortization of such payments as a reduction of sales. Such payments are capitalized when there are distinct rights obtained and there are sufficient incremental cash flows to support the recoverability of the assets established.
finding: RTX treats payments for platform exclusivity as a price discount (a reduction of sales) and only capitalises them when enough incremental cash flow is expected, so buying a sole-source position is in effect priced as a discount.

quote: additional payments are due to Rolls-Royce contingent upon each hour flown through June 2027 by the V2500-powered aircraft in service as of the acquisition date. These flight hour payments are being capitalized as collaboration assets and amortized to cost of sales.
finding: The IAE buyout was structured as a per-flight-hour earn-out to Rolls-Royce until June 2027, so P&W pays RR only as the V2500 fleet flies. This is a way to share usage risk in a partnership exit.

quote: For both our commercial aerospace collaboration assets and exclusivity arrangements, the pattern of economic benefit generally results in no amortization during the development period with amortization beginning as programs enter full rate production and aftermarket cycles.
finding: RTX's accounting assumes that engine programmes create value only once they reach full-rate production and the aftermarket, not during development.

quote: In our commercial engine and wheels and brakes businesses, when the OEM product is sold for a loss, but the combined OEM and aftermarket arrangement for each individual sales campaign is profitable, we record OEM product losses at the time of product delivery.
finding: P&W knowingly sells commercial engines below cost when the combined OE plus aftermarket campaign is profitable, and books the OE loss engine by engine at delivery. Each campaign is judged on lifecycle value.

quote: In our Collins Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney businesses, we may offer customers incentives to purchase our products, which may result in payments made to those customers, which are treated as a reduction in sales.
finding: P&W pays cash incentives to customers to win engine purchases and treats them as price reductions, one channel for aggressive terms.

quote: In view of the risks and costs associated with developing new engines and the large up-front investments required that often require returns generated over the full estimated life of the engine, Pratt & Whitney has entered into certain collaboration arrangements in which sales, costs and risks are shared.
finding: RTX states that new-engine returns come only over the engine's full life, and this long payback is why P&W shares programmes with partners.

quote: Pratt & Whitney is the principal participant in all existing collaborative arrangements, with the exception of the Engine Alliance (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation, which markets and manufactures the GP7000 engine for the Airbus A380 aircraft. There are no individually significant collaborative arrangements, and none of the collaborators individually have more than a 25 % share
finding: P&W leads all its engine collaborations except the GP7000 joint venture with GE on the A380, and caps any single partner at 25% (the FY2020 and FY2016 filings gave 31%). It is willing to co-own a widebody engine with a rival.

quote: We extend performance and operating cost guarantees beyond our normal service and warranty policies for extended periods on some of our products, particularly commercial aircraft engines. Liability under such guarantees is based upon future product performance and durability. ... In addition, we incur discretionary costs to service our products in connection with product performance issues.
finding: P&W sells commercial engines with extended performance and operating cost guarantees and pays discretionary costs when products underperform, so the durability risk sits with P&W.

quote: Pratt & Whitney holds a 61 % program share interest in the International Aero Engines AG (IAE) collaboration with MTU Aero Engines AG (MTU) and Japanese Aero Engines Corporation (JAEC) and a 49.5 % ownership interest in IAE.
finding: After buying out Rolls-Royce, P&W controls the V2500 programme with a 61% programme share, with MTU and JAEC as the minority partners.

quote: Pratt & Whitney, JAEC and MTU are participants in International Aero Engines, LLC (IAE LLC), whose business purpose is to coordinate ... product support for the PW1100G-JM engine for the Airbus A320neo aircraft ... Pratt & Whitney holds a 59 % program share interest and a 59 % ownership interest in IAE LLC.
finding: P&W carried the V2500 partnership model onto the A320neo GTF: it keeps control (59%) but gives about 41% of the PW1100G-JM programme to MTU and JAEC.

quote: The extent to which the financing commitments will be utilized is not currently known, since customers may be able to obtain more favorable terms from other financing sources. ... Our financing commitments with customers are contingent upon maintenance of certain levels of financial condition by the customers.
finding: RTX's customer financing is a backstop rather than cheap money: it is priced at market and conditional on customer creditworthiness, which limits how far P&W buys orders with financing.

quote: amortization, were approximately $2.6 billion, and our remaining estimated commitments, net of collaborator share, were approximately $6.2 billion. We regularly assess the recoverability of these intangibles, which is dependent upon our
finding: At end-2022 RTX had $2.6bn of exclusivity assets for platform positions and $6.2bn more committed net of partners; by end-2023 this was $3.1bn paid and $5.7bn still committed.

quote: IAE and IAE LLC retain limited equity with the primary economics of the programs passed to the participants. As such, we have determined that IAE and IAE LLC are variable interest entities with Pratt & Whitney as the primary beneficiary.
finding: The V2500 and PW1100G-JM consortia pass their economics to members, with P&W as controlling beneficiary, the model P&W uses to share narrowbody engine programmes.

quote: In view of the risks and costs associated with developing new engines, Pratt & Whitney has entered into collaboration arrangements in which revenues, costs, and risks are shared with third parties. At December 31, 2023, the interests of third-party collaboration participants in Pratt & Whitney-directed jet engine programs ranged, in the aggregate per program, from 13% to 49%.
finding: P&W persisted through 2023 in sharing 13-49% of each engine programme's revenues, costs and risks with partners rather than funding new engines alone, the same range as in earlier years.

quote: The evolving nature of these standards, along with the long duration of development, production, and aftermarket support programs, creates uncertainty regarding program profitability, particularly with our aircraft engine products.
finding: RTX singles out aircraft engines as the products whose long development-to-aftermarket life cycles make programme profitability most uncertain.

quote: Highly competitive activity within the commercial aerospace industry has included substantial discounts and other financial incentives, performance and operating cost guarantees, and participation in financing arrangements, in order ... to secure both new engine business and the aftermarket revenues associated with these products.
finding: Engine campaigns are won with deep discounts, performance guarantees and financing to lock in the aftermarket, i.e. P&W prices new engines to capture lifetime service revenue.

quote: the possibility exists that competitors or customers will develop aftermarket services and parts for our products that attract customers and adversely impact our return on investment on new products.
finding: P&W's return on a new engine depends on capturing its aftermarket, so third-party parts and services are seen as a direct threat to new-programme economics.

quote: At times, our aerospace businesses also enter into firm fixed-price or cost-share development contracts with customers, which may require us to bear cost overruns related to unforeseen technical and design challenges that arise during the development and early production stages of the program.
finding: RTX aerospace businesses accept fixed-price or cost-share development terms with customers, bearing development overruns themselves.

quote: Also included within intangible assets are exclusivity assets, which are payments made to secure certain contractual rights to provide products on new commercial aerospace platforms. At December 31, 2023, our exclusivity assets, net of accumulated amortization, were approximately $3.1 billion, and our remaining estimated commitments, net of collaborator share, were approximately $5.7 billion.
finding: RTX pays to secure contractual rights to supply new commercial aircraft platforms: $3.1bn capitalised by end-2023 and $5.7bn more committed net of partners.

quote: We assess the recoverability of these intangibles, which is dependent upon our assumptions around the future success and profitability of the underlying aircraft platforms, including the associated aftermarket revenue streams, and the related future cash flows.
finding: Exclusivity payments are justified by the platform's success and its aftermarket stream, confirming that P&W buys positions to earn service revenue.

quote: In our commercial engine and wheels and brakes businesses, when the OEM product is sold for a loss, but the combined OEM and aftermarket arrangement for each individual sales campaign is profitable, we record OEM product losses at the time of product delivery.
finding: P&W judges engine sales campaign by campaign on OE plus aftermarket together, and knowingly sells OE engines at a loss when the combined campaign is profitable.

quote: In view of the risks and costs associated with developing new engines and the large up-front investments required that often require returns generated over the full estimated life of the engine, Pratt & Whitney has entered into certain collaboration arrangements in which sales, costs, and risks are shared.
finding: P&W explains that new engines need large up-front investment repaid only over the engine's whole life, which is why it shares programmes with partners.

quote: Pratt & Whitney is the principal participant in all existing collaborative arrangements, with the exception of the Engine Alliance (EA), a joint venture with GE Aviation, which provides aftermarket support, spare parts, and service for the GP7000 engine for the Airbus A380 aircraft... none of the collaborators individually have more than a 25 % share
finding: P&W keeps control of its collaborations (no partner above 25%), the one exception being the Engine Alliance JV with GE on the A380 GP7000, a precedent for teaming with a rival engine maker on a widebody.

quote: We extend performance and operating cost guarantees beyond our normal service and warranty policies for extended periods on some of our products, particularly commercial aircraft engines. Liability under such guarantees is based upon future product performance and durability.
finding: P&W sells commercial engines with extended performance and operating cost guarantees, so durability shortfalls become its own liability.

quote: Pratt & Whitney holds a 61 % program share interest in the International Aero Engines AG (IAE) collaboration with MTU Aero Engines AG (MTU) and Japanese Aero Engines Corporation (JAEC)... Pratt & Whitney holds a 59 % program share interest and a 59 % ownership interest in IAE LLC.
finding: P&W runs both the V2500 (IAE) and the PW1100G-JM (IAE LLC) as consortia with MTU and JAEC, keeping a controlling majority share.

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s net program share interest in IAE and IAE LLC, after considering its sub-collaborator share, is 57 % and 51 %, respectively.
finding: After sub-collaborators, P&W's economic share is 57% of the V2500 and only 51% of the A320neo GTF, so it keeps just over half of GTF profits and losses.

quote: Many of our aerospace customers are covered under long-term aftermarket service agreements at both Collins and Pratt & Whitney, which are inclusive of both spare parts and services.
finding: Many P&W customers buy their aftermarket through long-term service agreements that bundle spare parts and services.

quote: If we fail in our development projects or if our new products or technologies fail to achieve customer acceptance or competitors develop more capable technologies or offerings, we may be unsuccessful in obtaining new contracts or winning all or a portion of next generation programs, including in key areas such as advanced sensing solutions, next-generation aircraft engine technologies
finding: New in the FY2024 filing: RTX names next-generation aircraft engine technologies as an area where it could lose all or part of next-generation programmes to more capable rivals.

quote: At December 31, 2024, our exclusivity assets, net of accumulated amortization, were approximately $3.3 billion, and our remaining estimated commitments, net of collaborator share, were approximately $5.5 billion.
finding: RTX kept buying platform exclusivity: $3.3bn capitalised by end-2024 (from $2.6bn in 2022) with $5.5bn still committed net of partners.

quote: Christopher T. Calio President (since March 2023), Chief Executive Officer (since May 2024) and Director, RTX Corporation (since December 2023) Chief Operating Officer, RTX Corporation; President, Pratt & Whitney; President, Commercial Engines, Pratt & Whitney
finding: RTX's CEO from May 2024 is a former president of Pratt & Whitney and of its commercial engines business.

GS's P&W commercial aftermarket revenue (ex-GTF) was $8,545mn in 2015 and $12,182mn in 2019, fell 34% to $8,040mn in 2020, then recovered to $8,728mn (2021), $10,953mn (2022), $13,035mn (2023) and $14,534mn (2024).

GS's GTF power-by-the-hour block assumes 3,000 narrowbody flight hours a year, 98% of engines on wing, 0.8% of hours captured in PBH and a $150 per-hour PBH rate, giving annual PBH revenue of $0.003528mn (about $3,528) per engine.
implication: (inference) GS treats hourly PBH as a minor revenue stream; almost all GTF aftermarket value in its model comes from time-and-material overhauls and life-limited parts.

finding: GS's GTF aftermarket plugs are a $3mn overhaul, a 35% aftermarket margin and 3% annual aftermarket pricing, with timing weights 'PBH yr 5/6/7' of 0.3/0.4/0.3 and 'LLP yr 7/8' of 0.5/0.5.
implication: (inference) The GTF overhaul line (row 21) reconciles exactly to half of each delivery cohort taking a $3mn LLP overhaul in year 7 and half in year 8 (delivery year = year 1), escalated 3%/yr from 2017 (e.g. 2022 = 124 x 0.5 x 3 x 1.03^5 = $215.6mn); the PBH line reconciles to cohort x weight x years-in-service x $3,528 x escalation at a first shop visit in years 5-7. At $3mn and 35% margin one LLP overhaul earns ~$1.05mn of EBIT, about one engine's 2024 OE loss (~$1.0mn) but received 6-7 years later; payback needs later shop visits too.

finding: GS's overhaul block lists '1st refurb' at 7.33 and '2nd refurb' at 4.67 (units not labelled).
implication: (inference) Consistent with 22,000 and 14,000 hours between refurbishments at 3,000 hours a year, i.e. first shop visit after ~7 years and the second ~4.7 years later; GS's LLP overhaul timing (years 7-8) is in the same range.

finding: GS models about 62,555 P&W Canada engines in service in 2019 rising to 68,000 in 2025E, against about 12,435 large commercial engines in 2019 rising to 17,500 in 2025E.
implication: (inference) GS's P&W Canada series matches the 64,000 (2019) and 'over 70,000' (2025) installed base to which P&W applied its 9% annual shop-visit induction rule (rtx_transcripts p1023), so that rule belongs to the small-engine fleet: 9% of 68,000 is about 6,100 visits a year. P&W's own large-commercial target of about 2,600 shop visits in 2025 on GS's 17,500 engines implies roughly 15% a year, a different rate.

finding: GS's in-service fleet assumptions for P&W are 10,500 large commercial engines in 2016 growing to 12,435 in 2019 and 17,500 in 2025E, 7,500 military engines (2016) rising to 8,000 (2020), and 60,000 P&W Canada engines (2016) rising to 68,000 (2025E).
GS projects the GTF installed base at 6,571 engines in 2025E, 7,747 in 2026E, 9,017 in 2027E and 10,388 in 2028E.
GS's GTF PBH aftermarket revenue is $0.72mn in 2020, $7.63mn in 2022, $16.08mn in 2024, $17.26mn in 2025E and $30.64mn in 2028E.

GS's GTF overhaul aftermarket revenue starts in 2022 at $216mn (zero through 2021), rising to $786mn in 2023, $1,625mn in 2024 and $2,479mn in 2025E, dips to $2,416mn (2026E) and $2,256mn (2027E), then reaches $2,772mn in 2028E.
implication: (inference) The 2026-27 dip mirrors the 2020 delivery trough working through the year-7/8 overhaul lag: aftermarket revenue echoes OE volumes with a long delay.

finding: GS's GTF aftermarket EBIT is $78mn in 2022, $280mn in 2023, $574mn in 2024, $874mn in 2025E, $852mn in 2026E, $798mn in 2027E and $981mn in 2028E.

GS estimates GTF unit production cost fell from $6.95mn per engine in 2016 (first 124 deliveries) to $5.07mn in 2017, $4.31mn in 2018 and $3.97mn in 2019 (about 738 deliveries), a 43% reduction in three years.
implication: (inference) A new engine starts at roughly 2.5x its net price in unit cost and needs several hundred units a year to walk down the learning curve; early-ramp OE losses are steep.

finding: GS estimates the OE loss (dilution) on each GTF delivered was $4.2mn in 2016, $2.32mn in 2017, $1.56mn in 2018 and $1.22mn in 2019.
implication: (inference) P&W accepted OE losses of $1-4mn per engine in the first four years of a new narrowbody engine; a next-generation launch should expect similar launch-year losses.

finding: GS's total commercial OE dilution (GTF plus V2500) grew from $250mn in 2014 and $400mn in 2015 to $691mn in 2016, $832mn in 2017, $975mn in 2018 and $936mn in 2019.
GS carries a $0.4mn OE loss on every V2500 delivered, while V2500 deliveries ran down from 621 in 2014 and 558 in 2015 to 426.4 in 2016, 250.3 in 2017, 91 in 2019 and 0 in 2021.
implication: (inference) Even a mature engine (V2500) is modelled as OE-loss-making; the IAE/V2500 value sits in the aftermarket of the installed base.

finding: GS models the GTF at a $11mn list price with a 75% discount, giving a net OE price of $2.75mn per engine held flat from 2015 to 2020 (K12 2.75) and then escalated 3% a year from 2021 (L12 2.7775).
implication: (inference) In GS's view P&W sold the GTF at about a quarter of list price to win A320neo/A220/E2 positions, i.e. it buys the installed base with deep OE concessions and recovers value in the aftermarket; aggressive terms are the norm, not the exception.

finding: GS's GTF net price per engine rises from $2.86mn in 2022 and $3.04mn in 2024 to $3.13mn in 2025E and $3.42mn in 2028E.
GS's GTF cost per engine rose to $4.36mn in 2020 (from $3.97mn in 2019) and then declines about 1% a year: $4.28mn in 2021, $4.07mn in 2024, $4.03mn in 2025E and $3.91mn in 2028E.
GS's GTF OE loss per engine went back up to $1.61mn in 2020, then narrows from $1.50mn (2021) to $1.03mn (2024), $0.90mn (2025E), $0.77mn (2026E) and $0.49mn (2028E).
implication: (inference) Even 12 years after entry into service GS does not have the GTF OE line reaching breakeven; OE losses persist for well over a decade.

finding: GS's commercial OE dilution stays near $0.8-1.0bn a year ($821mn in 2020, $934mn in 2021, $917mn in 2022), peaks at $1,044mn in 2023 and $1,039mn in 2024, then eases to $979mn (2025E), $798mn (2027E) and $672mn (2028E).
implication: (inference) Because deliveries keep growing as per-unit losses shrink, the absolute OE drag stays around $1bn a year for a decade; the OE penalty of a new engine is a long, flat plateau, not a short spike.

finding: GS's platform build models P&W's A320neo engine deliveries at a 40% share ('A320neo @ 40%'): 54.4 engines in 2016, 308.8 in 2018, 440.8 in 2019, 344.8 in 2020, 448.56 in 2021, 464.08 in 2022 and 456.8 in 2023.
implication: (inference) GS treats P&W as the minority A320neo supplier (~40% vs CFM LEAP ~60%); the GTF's share of A320neo deliveries is the variable a durability upgrade would try to defend.

finding: GS's 2015 P&W EBIT build is military $378mn, commercial OE -$700mn and commercial aftermarket $2,222mn, totalling $1,899mn (13.5% margin) vs $1,891mn in the main model.
GS's net GTF/V2500 OE-plus-aftermarket impact on P&W EBIT (before GTF R&D) was -$250mn in 2014, -$400mn in 2015, -$691mn in 2016, -$832mn in 2017, -$975mn in 2018 and -$936mn in 2019.
GS attributes GTF R&D/E&D expense of $400mn in 2014, $300mn a year in 2015-2017 and $200mn a year in 2018-2019 to P&W's EBIT.

In the GS GTF analysis, P&W total EBIT fell from $2,129mn in 2014 to $1,934mn in 2019, while EBIT excluding the GTF/V2500 OE and aftermarket impact rose from $2,379mn to $2,870mn and EBIT before both that impact and GTF R&D rose from $2,779mn to $3,070mn.
implication: (inference) GS's reading: the rest of P&W grew profit through 2014-19, and the GTF launch absorbed about $1.1bn of EBIT a year by 2019; P&W chose to carry that drag to win share.

finding: GS's 2019 P&W EBIT build is military $576mn, commercial OE -$1,136mn, commercial aftermarket ex-GTF $2,497mn and GTF aftermarket $0mn, totalling $1,938mn (9.3% margin) vs $1,934mn in the main model.
implication: (inference) Commercial aftermarket (ex-GTF) earned about 20% of its revenue in 2019 in GS's build and had to cover a $1.1bn commercial OE loss; the aftermarket funds the OE war.

finding: GS's 2020 P&W EBIT build is military $660mn, commercial OE -$896mn, commercial aftermarket ex-GTF $643mn and GTF aftermarket $0.25mn, totalling $408mn (2.4% margin) vs $426mn in the main model.
implication: (inference) When COVID cut commercial aftermarket profit by about three-quarters, military profit kept P&W positive; the defence business is P&W's shock absorber.

finding: In the GS GTF analysis P&W EBIT was $426mn in 2020 vs $1,246mn ex-GTF, $487mn vs $1,420mn in 2021, $1,688mn vs $2,453mn in 2023 and $2,068mn vs $2,533mn in 2024.

GS's 2024 P&W EBIT build is military $724mn, commercial OE -$1,039mn, commercial aftermarket ex-GTF $2,192mn and GTF aftermarket $574mn, totalling $2,450mn (9.3% margin) vs $2,281mn in the main model.
GS's GTF R&D/E&D line drops to $75mn in 2020, $150mn in 2021 and $100mn in 2022-2023, and is zero from 2024.
implication: (inference) GTF development spend was cut hardest in 2020 (to $75mn from $200mn) when COVID hit P&W profit, i.e. programme R&D was a flexible lever in the crisis.

finding: GS's RTX free-cash-flow build carries GTF powder-metal cash outflows of $300mn in 2023, $2,300mn in 2024, $1,200mn in 2025E, $700mn in 2026E and zero from 2027E (about $4.5bn in total), against RTX FCF of $4,752mn in 2024 and $7,523mn in 2025E.
implication: (inference) GTF customer compensation is a multi-year cash drain peaking at roughly half of RTX's 2024 FCF, paid while RTX continued returning capital; a durability crisis costs P&W several billion dollars spread over ~4 years.

finding: GS's net GTF impact on P&W EBIT is -$820mn in 2020, -$933mn in 2021, -$839mn in 2022, -$765mn in 2023, -$465mn in 2024 and -$105mn in 2025E, reaching breakeven in 2027E (-$0.3mn) and turning positive at +$309mn in 2028E.
implication: (inference) In GS's view the GTF programme turns EBIT-positive only about 12 years after entry into service (2016 EIS, 2028E breakeven): a next-generation engine launched in the game would be a >10-year payback bet.

finding: GS's GTF analysis has P&W EBIT of $2,655mn in 2025E vs $2,761mn ex-GTF, $2,934mn vs $2,982mn in 2026E, and $3,565mn vs $3,256mn in 2028E, when the GTF becomes accretive.

GS's 2028E P&W EBIT build is military $793mn, commercial OE -$672mn, commercial aftermarket ex-GTF $3,104mn and GTF aftermarket $981mn, totalling $4,206mn (12.6% margin) vs $3,640mn in the main model.
GS's platform build has A220 GTF engines of 64 in 2018, 96 in 2019, 76 in 2020 and 136 in 2023, E2 engines of 28 (2019) and 70 (2023), and a platform GTF total of 564.8 (2019) and 662.8 (2023).
implication: (inference) P&W is sole source on A220 and E2 but these are small volumes; the A320neo split dominates GTF volume.

finding: GS's FCF build attributes $300m (2023) and $2.30bn (2024) of GTF powder-metal cash outflow to RTX, against reported-basis FCF in the build of $5.41bn and $4.75bn.
implication: (inference) The 2024 powder-metal cash cost equalled about half of that year's FCF ($4.75bn), or a third of FCF before it; RTX paid it from operating cash without cutting the dividend.

finding: GS models the GTF powder-metal cash cost falling to $1.20bn in 2025E and $700m in 2026E and ending ($0) in 2027E-2028E, for a 2023-2026E total of $4.5bn.
implication: (inference) GS expects the crisis cash drain to be over by the start of the game (2026-28 turn), freeing about $2bn a year versus 2024.

finding: GS projects GTF deliveries growing 8% a year: 1089 in 2025E, 1176 in 2026E, 1270 in 2027E and 1371 in 2028E.

GS's GTF Analysis sheet is not reconciled to its segment model after 2023: its top-line P&W revenue shows $18,845mn for 2024 against $28,066mn in SEG, its OE/AM build totals $26,283mn, and its check row shows gaps of -$1,783mn (2024), -$3,270mn (2025E) and -$6,951mn (2028E).
implication: (inference) Treat the GTF per-engine economics as GS's structural view rather than a reconciled forecast; use SEG for P&W totals.

finding: GS's 2019 P&W revenue build is $20,902mn: military $5,763mn (OE 1,657, aftermarket 4,106) and commercial $15,140mn (OE 2,957, aftermarket ex-GTF 12,182, GTF aftermarket 0); commercial aftermarket is 58.3% of the total.

GS's 2024 P&W revenue build is $26,283mn: military $6,891mn (OE 1,709, aftermarket 5,182) and commercial $19,392mn (OE 3,217, aftermarket ex-GTF 14,534, GTF aftermarket 1,641); commercial aftermarket incl. GTF is 61.5% and commercial OE 12.2% of the total.
implication: (inference) P&W is an aftermarket business carrying a loss-making OE line: in GS's split commercial aftermarket is ~5x commercial OE revenue.

finding: GS's P&W revenue build grows commercial OE 6% in 2025E, 6% in 2026E, 5.5% in 2027E and 5% in 2028E, and commercial aftermarket ex-GTF 8%, 7%, 7% and 6.5%.
GS forecasts P&W revenue of $8,515mn in 4Q25E, $31,935mn in 2025E, $34,904mn in 2026E and $40,447mn in 2028E, with adjusted operating income of $2,673mn, $3,012mn and $3,640mn (9.0% margin in 2028E).

GS models P&W organic growth of 12.5% in 4Q25E, 13.8% in 2025E, 9.3% in 2026E, 8.2% in 2027E and 7.1% in 2028E, with adjusted margins of 8.4% (2025E) and 8.6% (2026E) and an incremental margin of 10.9% in 2027E.
implication: (inference) GS expects only ~0.2-0.3 points of margin expansion a year at P&W through 2028: the GTF recovery is slow, which limits P&W's appetite and capacity for another loss-leading launch before the 2030s.

finding: GS forecasts P&W at 35.7% of RTX revenue in 2025E and 37.8% in 2028E, and 24.8% and 26.4% of adjusted operating income.

speaker: analyst (UBS)
quote: there was some commentary by some of your competitors about aggressive pricing as you're trying to "hold share" through some of the early execution issues. Any comments on that?
finding: Rivals claimed P&W priced the GTF aggressively to hold A320neo share during its early problems; the CFO denied it and described deliberate restraint (next item).
trigger: competitor claims of aggressive GTF pricing

speaker: analyst (Barclays)
quote: you reached an agreement with Spirit Airlines in the quarter that was made public. Is that amount kind of on a per AOG basis representative of your other customer agreements? Because that would seem to imply a higher compensation number than you've baked into your forecast.
finding: An analyst argued the public Spirit Airlines settlement implied higher GTF compensation than P&W's provision.

speaker: analyst (Morgan Stanley)
quote: do you think there's an opportunity to maybe improve on the $1 billion-or-so OE loss that you've talked about? Your partner in MTU has highlighted sort of breakeven OE economics at some point next decade from lost discounts and automation benefits.
finding: Analysts, citing GTF partner MTU, suggested the roughly $1B annual GTF OE loss could reach breakeven next decade; Hayes rejected OE breakeven (next item).

speaker: analyst (Jefferies)
quote: as part of the proxy, you provided some long-term forecasts for Pratt. Specifically in 2023, EBIT margins for the large commercial business are expected to generate 7% margins.
finding: The merger proxy disclosed a planned ~7% EBIT margin for P&W's large commercial engine business in 2023; management confirmed the figure applies to LCE, not all of P&W (next item).

doc: UTC Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna conference, Sep 2019)
speaker: analyst (Morgan Stanley)
quote: On the GTF, what do you think is the biggest risk in getting that aftermarket goodness over the next 10, 20, 30 years? It's so hard for us to get comfortable with this especially with the $1 billion OE loss
finding: Analysts framed the GTF as carrying roughly a $1B annual OE loss to be recovered by a 10-30 year aftermarket; Hayes' answer (next item) did not dispute the figure.

speaker: analyst (UBS, Myles Walton)
quote: how does the cumulative negative margin relate to that, I guess, $1.2 billion that you all had talked about as being sort of the level of the 2018, 2019 period? How much higher is it?
finding: The analyst cites about $1.2B a year of GTF negative engine margin in 2018-19; the CFO confirmed the peak would be only 'a little higher, not much'.

speaker: analyst (UBS, Myles Walton)
quote: could you talk about the losses that you're currently incurring per unit? How much of an improvement the cost reduction efforts are actually translating to unit costs? And then maybe just as you look at the glide slope of losses on the engine, I think the prior comments were around peaking in 2025.

quote: Pratt & Whitney has inserted the gearbox between the low pressure turbine and the inlet fan which has enabled the engine designers to increase the size of fan blade which, in turn, has enabled them to almost double the bypass ratio from 6:1 in a typical V2500 to about 12:1 in the PW1100G.
finding: P&W chose a radical architecture change (a fan gearbox, doubling bypass ratio to about 12:1) rather than CFM's incremental approach.

speaker: David L. Calhoun, President & CEO (Boeing)
quote: we have a gap. We got room to make up, and we're going to get there, but it's going to be at a constrained rate ... they are not going to be rate limiters, either short term or long term. It will boil down to engines and the competition for castings between Pratt and CFM.
finding: Boeing's CEO said the binding limit on 737 rates would be engines and the competition between Pratt and CFM for the same castings supply: an airframer-side confirmation that P&W's castings supply, and so its output, is squeezed when CFM ramps.

quote: when the Airbus company decided that it wanted to launch its new airplane, the NEO, and we could not make a business case to launch a new engine for the NEO. Pratt & Whitney was in a different phase of development with respect to their new engine, and they felt they could. So it put the partnership out of alignment
finding: Per its IAE partner, P&W committed a new engine to the A320neo on its own technology readiness when RR could not make a business case for one, and accepted that this put the IAE partnership out of alignment rather than wait for the partner.

response: P&W, further along with its new engine (the GTF), offered it for the neo anyway, splitting the IAE partnership
