quote: your customer base had the previous style of engine, the V2500, and on a go-forward basis, with new airplanes coming aboard, they ... wanted to take advantage of the new Pratt & Whitney engine. So it became very, very difficult, very hard to go in and renegotiate contracts with airlines
finding: Per RR, once P&W's new engine was on offer, the V2500 airline customers wanted it for their new aircraft, which made it very hard for the IAE partnership to renegotiate long-term V2500 contracts: P&W's new product pulled demand away from the partnership's legacy engine.
trigger: P&W's new engine became available for new A320-family aircraft
response: IAE customers sought the new P&W engine, undermining V2500 contract renegotiation and the partnership

doc: FY 2011 Earnings Call (RR 2011 Fixed Income Call, 9 Feb 2012)
speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director (Rolls-Royce)
quote: we announced the restructuring of IAE, where we look to sell our equity shareholding of 32.5%, realizing the value of our investment. And we will continue to be a subcontractor in the existing arrangement. And at the same time, announcing a new JV with Pratt & Whitney for the future midsize market.
finding: Per Rolls-Royce, the IAE restructuring (RR selling its 32.5% equity and staying a V2500 subcontractor) was paired with a new Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce JV for the future midsize market: P&W's only precedent for agreeing to co-develop a next-generation narrowbody-class engine with RR.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO (Rolls-Royce)
quote: The third major decision was a sale of our financial holding in IAE, surprising many with the embedded value. At the same time, we announced plans to form a new joint venture with Pratt & Whitney to build engines for the next generation of midsized aircraft.
finding: The planned P&W-RR JV, announced with the IAE sale, was scoped to build engines for the next generation of midsized aircraft, and RR's CEO ranked the IAE sale plus the JV among RR's three major decisions of 2011.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO (Rolls-Royce)
quote: the new joint venture that we've established or will establish we hope with Pratt & Whitney, which gives us access back into this very large and important market in the future.
finding: RR saw the JV with P&W as its route back into the narrowbody market, but in February 2012 it was not yet in place ('established or will establish we hope'): P&W, as incumbent, held the gate to RR's narrowbody re-entry.

speaker: James M. Guyette, CEO Rolls-Royce North America (IAE board member)
quote: So we've all felt that the best way forward was for us to move out of the partnership ... Take in the $1.5 billion. Have the revenue stream, going forward on power by the hour. And also, maintain our industrial position. But then, even more importantly, to make sure that the partnership could reform for the next narrow-body airplane.
finding: The IAE split was resolved by the non-launching partner leaving for $1.5bn plus a power-by-the-hour revenue stream while keeping its industrial work, and RR said the exit was structured so that the partnership could re-form for the next narrowbody aircraft.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO (Rolls-Royce)
quote: We completed the sale of our shareholding in June and received a consideration of GBP 1.5 billion of cash... The new joint venture for the next generation of midsized aircraft with Pratt & Whitney and the other IAE partners remains subject to regulatory approval.
finding: By July 2012 the IAE buy-out had closed (RR paid GBP 1.5bn in June) but the next-generation midsize JV, now described as including P&W and the other IAE partners, was still awaiting regulatory approval: the cash deal closed first and the co-development JV lagged.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO (Rolls-Royce)
quote: we exited because, in all joint ventures, you need to have alignment between the partners, and because we were only on the old engine and not on the new engine and the other partners were on both the old and the new, we no longer had alignment.
finding: RR's later account: IAE broke up because P&W and the other partners were on both the old V2500 and the new engine while RR was only on the old one; a JV with P&W holds only while both partners are on the same new engine.
In 1Q20 the group repaid $13.8bn of long-term debt, cutting gross debt from $43.3bn at end-2019 to $28.8bn and net debt from $38.3bn to $22.6bn; treasury stock fell from -$32.6bn to -$10.4bn by 2Q20.
implication: (inference) RTX entered COVID with net debt cut by about $15bn at the separation and merger, which let it keep the dividend and protect R&D through 2020.

finding: Around the 2020 UTC-Raytheon merger, goodwill rose from $36.6bn (4Q19) to $53.3bn (2Q20), intangibles from $24.5bn (2019) to $40.5bn (2020), equity from $41.9bn to $72.2bn, and common stock from $23.0bn to $36.7bn (2Q20).
implication: (inference) The merger was paid in shares, not cash: equity rose about $30bn and the group did not take on acquisition debt.

finding: RTX's net debt/EBITDA was 2.76x (2020), 2.42x (2021), 2.54x (2022) and 2.54x (2024); debt/capital fell from 50.8% (2019) to 30.6% (2020), then rose to 42.3% (2023) and was 40.7% in 2024.
RTX repaid $2.50bn of long-term debt in 2024 and $780m and $1.50bn in 2Q25 and 3Q25; net debt fell from $37.2bn at 2Q25 to $33.1bn at 3Q25.
implication: (inference) After the 2023 debt-funded buyback, RTX used 2024-25 cash to repay debt rather than buy back stock.
(inference) RTX runs with a modest cash buffer of $5-9bn and relies on cash generation and debt markets, not a cash pile, to fund large outlays.

finding: RTX's expensed R&D (income-statement line) fell from $3.25bn in 2018 and $3.19bn in 2019 to $2.69bn in 2020, a 15% cut, taking R&D from 4.7% of sales to 4.2%.
implication: (inference) In COVID RTX cut R&D by about $0.5bn, roughly in line with sales, while it kept the dividend per share at $1.90; R&D is a flexible line, the dividend is not.

finding: RTX bought back $1.33bn of shares in 2018 and $800m in 2019, almost stopped in 2020 ($47m), and resumed with $2.33bn in 2021 and $2.80bn in 2022.
implication: (inference) Buybacks, not the dividend, are RTX's shock absorber: they went to near zero in the 2020 crisis.

finding: In 2023 RTX repurchased $12.87bn of shares, $10.28bn of it in 4Q23, and issued $12.34bn of net long-term debt ($9.54bn in 4Q23), raising net debt from $25.7bn to $37.2bn.
implication: (inference) In the quarter after the powder-metal charge, RTX borrowed to retire shares (the diluted count then fell about 7%, from 1,440m in 2023 to 1,344m in 2024), signalling confidence and putting shareholders ahead of balance-sheet headroom.

finding: After COVID, RTX's expensed R&D stayed flat at $2.73bn (2021), $2.71bn (2022), $2.81bn (2023) and $2.93bn (2024), so it fell from 4.2% to 3.6% of sales as revenue grew.
implication: (inference) RTX did not restore pre-COVID R&D intensity during the GTF crisis; no step-up in self-funded R&D for a next-generation engine is visible through 2024.
(inference) Capex was the deepest cut in the COVID crisis (-38% vs R&D -15%), and by 2024 ($2.63bn) was still below its 2019 level.
(inference) The dividend was never cut, not in COVID nor in the powder-metal year: it is the first call on RTX cash, ahead of capex and R&D.

finding: Dividends paid rose from $2.50bn (2018) to $2.88bn (2019), $2.73bn (2020), $2.96bn (2021), $3.13bn (2022), $3.24bn (2023) and $3.22bn (2024); in 2023 they were 105% of reported net income.
RTX's diluted share count fell from 1,516m (2019 pro forma) to 1,486m (2022), 1,440m (2023) and 1,344m (2024).
implication: (inference) The 2023 accelerated buyback cut the diluted count by about 7% between 2023 and 2024 (1,440m to 1,344m), against only 2% over 2019-2022 (1,516m to 1,486m).

finding: RTX's investment in collaboration intangible assets rose from $172m (2020), $188m (2021) and $218m (2022) to $570m (2023) and $611m (2024), then $104m, $122m and $121m in 1Q-3Q25.
implication: (inference) Collaboration intangibles are payments to programme partners (at RTX mainly engine collaborations); their near-tripling in 2023-24 suggests extra cash went to engine partners during the GTF crisis. GS models zero from 4Q25.

finding: RTX's quarterly dividend went from $0.475 (1Q21) to $0.51 (2Q21), $0.55 (2Q22), $0.59 (2Q23), $0.63 (2Q24) and $0.68 (2Q25), a raise each second quarter of 6.8-7.9%.
implication: (inference) The raise was kept on schedule in 2Q23 and 2Q24, either side of the powder-metal charge; the dividend is a fixed commitment.

finding: After the 2023 buyback, repurchases nearly stopped: $444m in 2024 ($294m of it in 3Q24), $50m in 1Q25 and nothing in 2Q-3Q25.
implication: (inference) RTX paused buybacks to pay powder-metal compensation and repay debt; it front-loaded returns in 2023, then deleveraged.

finding: RTX was a small net acquirer in 2020-2021 ($419m and $258m) but a net seller in 2024 ($1.80bn inflow from businesses) and 2025 ($1.19bn inflow in 3Q25).
implication: (inference) RTX funded part of its deleveraging by selling non-core businesses rather than by cutting the dividend.

finding: On GS's RTX pro-forma history, net sales grew from $50.6bn (2014) to $74.2bn (2019), and adjusted EBIT from $7.28bn to $8.99bn, after a peak of $9.78bn in 2018.
In 2020 RTX sales fell 13.7% to $64.1bn and reported EBIT swung from $8.45bn to a $838m loss, including a $3.18bn 'Charges & other' item in 2Q20; adjusted EBIT halved from $8.99bn to $4.18bn.

In 3Q23 RTX's net sales dropped to $13.46bn (from $18.32bn in 2Q23 and $19.93bn in 4Q23) and EBIT was -$1.40bn; GS's adjusted-earnings bridge adds back $3.00bn of 'Other adjustments' in that quarter (plus $104m of 'Adjustments in EBIT').
implication: (inference) GS treats the powder-metal charge as a one-off excluded from adjusted earnings, so the market judged RTX on underlying profit rather than on the charge.

finding: RTX group adjusted operating income was $11,326mn in 2019, $6,451mn in 2020, $8,895mn in 2023 and $10,183mn in 2024; reported operating income was -$821mn in 2020 and $3,561mn in 2023.
implication: (inference) Even in the two worst P&W years (2020, 2023) RTX's group adjusted profit stayed at $6-9bn; the parent's earnings capacity is the balance sheet behind P&W's engine bets.

finding: RTX sales recovered from $64.4bn (2021) to $67.1bn (2022), $68.9bn (2023) and $80.7bn (2024), with adjusted EBIT rising from $5.24bn to $6.02bn, $6.90bn and $9.68bn.
RTX adjusted EPS fell from $6.21 (2019 pro forma) to $3.29 (2020) and recovered to $4.27, $4.78, $5.04 and $5.73 in 2021-2024, still below 2019.

implication: (inference) Group FCF stayed at $4.5-5.5bn a year from 2021 to 2024, below 2019, while the GTF fleet problem was absorbing cash.

finding: RTX's FCF margin was 3.9% (2020), 7.8% (2021), 7.3% (2022), 7.9% (2023) and 5.6% (2024); FCF converted 59% of adjusted net income in 2024 vs 71% in 2019.

implication: (inference) Since the merger loaded the balance sheet with goodwill and intangibles, RTX's returns on capital are low single digits; a new engine programme will be judged against a group earning low single-digit ROIC on this measure.

finding: RTX's gross margin was 25.3% (2018) and 22.9% (2019), fell to 10.9% in 2020 and 17.5% in 2023, and recovered to 19.1% in 2024.
In 2025 to date RTX reported net sales of $20.31bn, $21.58bn and $22.48bn and EBIT of $2.04bn, $2.15bn and $2.52bn in 1Q-3Q, with 3Q25 adjusted EPS of $1.70.
In 2025 RTX generated operating cash flow of $1.31bn, $458m and $4.64bn in 1Q-3Q, and free cash flow of $792m, -$72m and $4.03bn.
RTX's net interest expense rose from $1.08bn (2019) and $1.28bn (2022) to $1.51bn (2023) and $1.86bn (2024), and ran at $443m and $449m a quarter in 1Q25 and 3Q25.
implication: (inference) Annual interest rose by about $0.6bn between 2022 and 2024, coinciding with the debt-funded 2023 buyback: returning cash early has a lasting cost.

finding: RTX built inventory by $1.58bn (2022), $1.10bn (2023) and $1.47bn (2024), while contract liabilities (customer advances) added $1.13bn (2020), $2.32bn (2023) and $1.87bn (2024) to cash.
implication: (inference) Customer advances largely financed the inventory build of the supply-chain years, so working capital did not limit investment.

finding: RTX's Aerospace backlog (P&W plus Collins) grew from $93bn at end-2021 to $106bn (2022), $118bn (2023), $125bn (2024) and $148bn at 3Q25, out of a total backlog of $251bn (Defense $103bn).
implication: (inference) A commercial backlog of about five years of P&W-plus-Collins sales gives RTX visibility to fund development without new orders.

finding: Sikorsky contributed $7.45bn of UTC sales in 2014 and $4.38bn in 2015, and nothing from 2016 (sales $0), after earning only $219m and $284m of operating profit in those years.
implication: (inference) UTC exited a low-margin aerospace business in 2015, during the GTF launch years; the parent prunes weak units rather than carry them.

finding: UTC's aerospace-systems business stepped up by acquisition: sales went from $4.76bn (2011) to $8.33bn (2012) and from $16.63bn (2018) to $26.03bn (2019), with operating profit rising from $2.30bn to $4.10bn in 2019.
implication: (inference) UTC's large capital deployment went into buying aerospace systems (2012 and 2018-19 steps), not into new engine programmes beyond the GTF.

finding: In 2019, legacy UTC had $77.05bn of sales including Otis ($13.11bn) and Climate, Controls & Security ($18.61bn), which the RTX pro-forma history excludes; RTX's 2019 pro-forma sales were $74.24bn, including legacy Raytheon's $29.18bn.
implication: (inference) The 2020 merger swapped UTC's commercial-building businesses ($4.6bn of 2019 operating profit) for Raytheon's defence business, so P&W is now funded by a group with a large defence cash flow.

Today's airlines are short of lift ... We're about the eighth or ninth year of V average life, and this is where the heavy maintenance overhauls are coming in.
finding: Airlines short of narrowbody lift, facing a 7-year backlog, were keeping older V2500 aircraft flying, feeding P&W's aftermarket.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: We have settled with Boeing on PFS 2. I won't go into the specifics other than to say, we think we've met all of their expectations for what we need to do from a cost standpoint. And they have met our expectations in terms of what we can do to guarantee future volumes on their airplanes.
finding: Boeing traded guaranteed future volumes for supplier cost-downs under PFS 2.
response: cost concessions for volume guarantees

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: cost pressure is continuous in aerospace ... probably more acute today on the narrow-body. We continue to work with Airbus to try and reduce costs. Obviously, the CSeries, the cost reduction will be paramount to Airbus. ... A piece of it goes to the bottom line, a piece of it goes to the customer.
finding: Airbus pushed suppliers hard on narrowbody and CSeries (A220) cost, and UTC shares its cost reductions between its own margin and the airframer.

speaker: Akhil Johri, EVP & CFO
quote: the reason why the Airbus 320neo and 737 MAX is doing so well from the airframers' perspective is because they had very little skin in the game. It is all on the back of the engine manufacturers, right.
finding: P&W's CFO viewed the A320neo and 737 MAX re-engines as airframer programmes where the engine makers carried most of the investment and risk.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: we're continuing to work with the Boeing company, both on the engine side as well as on the systems side. They've got some pretty tough cost targets out there. But they're optimistic about the market size. ... I don't think we see any announcements from us this year, probably not until the first part of next year.
finding: Boeing pressed suppliers, including engine makers, with tough cost targets for the NMA while being optimistic on market size; P&W expected no engine decision before early 2019.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So we've assumed roughly a 90-day production delay, which is consistent with direction that we've received from Boeing. ... And then in the back half of the year, we've essentially cut production in half from the rate that we had. So from 42 to 21.
finding: In January 2020 RTX planned on Boeing halting 737 MAX production for about 90 days and restarting at half rate (21 a month).

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: For Pratt OE, we expect our sales to decline in line with our main OEM customers, which is primarily Airbus for our large commercial engines. On the aftermarket side, GTF overhaul activity will continue as we upgrade engines to the latest configuration. However, legacy shop visits are now likely to be down 50% or more
finding: Airbus is P&W's main customer for large commercial engines, so P&W's OE volume follows Airbus production, while GTF upgrade overhauls continued regardless.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: it's tough right now for both Boeing and Airbus to place planes because of the financing constraints that some of their customers are under. Obviously, we'll work with Boeing and Airbus on that. But I really think it's that parked fleet returning to service first before you see a lot of new aircraft out there.
finding: RTX expected parked aircraft to return before new deliveries, with Boeing and Airbus struggling to place aircraft because of customer financing constraints.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: But the OEMs, of course, Boeing and Airbus, have a desire to build aircraft to keep their folks busy and to keep their cost in check. When you're going from building 63 A320s a month down to 35 or something like that, you can imagine the overhead cost balloon. ... we're expecting at least a 50% reduction in OE volume across Boeing and Airbus.
finding: RTX saw Boeing and Airbus as incentivized to keep building to absorb overhead, but planned on at least 50% lower OE volume as airlines did not need new aircraft.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: shifting to cash-conservation behaviors, which includes things such as deferring engine maintenance, requesting extended payment terms, deferring delivery of new aircraft and spare engines and requesting discounts on engine maintenance.
finding: In COVID airlines pressed P&W for deferred maintenance, extended payment terms, delayed deliveries and discounts on engine maintenance.

speaker: Anthony F. O'Brien, CFO
quote: The other point here, the early retirements that have been announced that folks have heard about, they're effectively pulling things forward by a year or 2, not call it 5 to 10 years. Some of the retirements could also get converted to cargo
finding: RTX judged that COVID fleet retirements only pulled old-fleet retirements forward by 1-2 years, limiting the hit to its legacy aftermarket.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: I would tell you that Pratt is fully aligned with Airbus deliveries this year and next year. We've been out -- we've talked to every single one of our customers who's going to be taking GTF-powered aircraft. ... that's about, as we would say, roughly a 40% reduction in GTF volume from the A320s in the next 1.5 years here.
finding: P&W aligned GTF output with Airbus's reduced A320 delivery plan after checking every GTF customer, accepting about a 40% volume cut over 1.5 years.
trigger: Airbus A320 production cuts in COVID
response: GTF production aligned to Airbus schedule, ~40% lower

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: But also it's the ramp that we're going to see and the production is slower, I think, than anybody had anticipated. On top of that, as Boeing has gone through and looked at the inventory levels that they have for all of our equipment
finding: RTX saw Boeing's 737 MAX production ramp as slower than anyone expected and Boeing carrying excess supplier inventory into 2021.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So we know people are deferring maintenance. That is they're using up green time on engines. ... We have to work with them to try and help them reduce maintenance costs in the near term.
finding: In COVID airlines burned engine green time to defer shop visits, and P&W chose to help them cut near-term maintenance cost rather than resist.
trigger: airlines deferring maintenance and using green time
response: work jointly with airlines to reduce near-term maintenance cost

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Narrow-bodies are coming back much more quickly. We see that in China. We see it in Europe. We see it in the U.S., whereas the widebody franchises are having a much more difficult time because they support international travel
finding: RTX saw the narrowbody market recovering well ahead of widebodies, which favoured P&W's narrowbody-only portfolio.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: As far as GTF cancellations, we haven't seen any. Obviously, Airbus is working with the customers as we are to make sure that we can continue to support the fleet that's out there as well as to continue to support the new deliveries this year and next, although they will be modest.
finding: P&W saw no GTF order cancellations in COVID and coordinated with Airbus on customer deliveries, which it expected to be modest.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Airbus has an active program on hydrogen. I suspect Boeing will as well. But again, we're sitting here in 2020. That is a 15-year time horizon.
finding: RTX saw Airbus as already committed to hydrogen and expected Boeing to follow, but treated it as a 15-year horizon.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: the airlines have done a lot in terms of cash conservation in 2020. They have deferred a lot of maintenance. They have diminished their inventory. So we're actually expecting to see a quicker rebound this time in the aftermarket than what we have seen historically
finding: RTX expected airlines' deferred maintenance and depleted spares stocks to bring a faster aftermarket rebound than in past cycles.

speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO (RTX)
quote: we started to see some retirements of some of the older engines out there... especially I think on the 112-inch. That's the 777 that we saw JAL retiring their fleet... But those engines will still end up in service someplace else, probably in a freighter configuration.
finding: RTX expected retired PW4000-powered 777s (e.g. JAL's) to find second lives as freighters, prolonging the legacy aftermarket.

speaker: Steve Timm, President, Collins Aerospace
quote: While we don't see a major new clean sheet on the immediate horizon, I will tell you we're very active with the OEMs on our technical road maps to make sure if our systems can contribute to that incremental 10 to 15 points of efficiency gain, we're surely there.
finding: In 2021 RTX saw no imminent clean-sheet airliner, but was working the OEMs' roadmaps for a next aircraft with a 10-15 point efficiency gain.

doc: Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference, Sep 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: Airbus has been very aggressive in trying to claim share... as Boeing has struggled... If Airbus really goes up to 75 airplanes a month as they are predicting, that would mean that Boeing's market share would be down somewhere around 35%... something that the Boeing company is not going to want to see.
finding: RTX reads Airbus's rate-75 plan as an aggressive share grab while Boeing struggles with the 737 MAX, and expects Boeing to resist falling to about 35% share.

doc: Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference, Sep 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: the production rates will creep up and probably back to that 110 a month... above that and then you get into problems in terms of the residual value of some of the aircraft. And so the leasing companies, I'm sure, are going to push back.
finding: RTX expects combined narrowbody output to settle around 110 a month, with lessors pushing back on higher rates to protect aircraft residual values.

doc: Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference, Sep 2021 (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: the one, I say, question mark out there is when the 787 gets back up to run rate production. As you know, it's down to about 5 a month, down from 12.
finding: RTX saw 787 output cut from 12 to about 5 a month by Boeing's factory issues, the main widebody-OE question mark.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: As far as 787, that, I think, is maybe the big question that we have right now. We are not shipping anything today on 787. We had expected to be delivering at about 5 a month.
finding: RTX saw Boeing's 787 production halted in late 2021 (no shipments versus a planned 5 a month), a key widebody-OE uncertainty.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: I think they're probably building at a rate of, what, 43 a month going up, we think, a little bit next year, and continuing on towards Guillaume's goal, I believe, of rate 75. Not clear we're going to get all the way to rate 75. But clearly, we see demand strengthening for the A320.
finding: RTX saw Airbus at about rate 43 on the A320 in late 2021 and doubted Airbus would reach its rate-75 goal, while acknowledging strengthening demand.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: They've got thousands of A320s in backlog. And the fact that there's a few parked, that's just really the state of the airline industry today that some of the airlines looking for financing, but we don't see any interruption in the production rate.
finding: RTX saw the parked A320s as an airline-financing issue, not a demand problem, given Airbus's backlog of thousands.

speaker: Greg Hayes, Chairman & CEO (RTX)
quote: while fuel prices are up, oil north of $80 a barrel, we believe that the airlines are being -- are able to pass along those higher fuel costs in the form of higher ticket prices. Obviously, if it's a prolonged increase, it does drive demand for next-generation aircraft.
finding: RTX expects only a sustained fuel-price rise to drive airline demand for next-generation (more fuel-efficient) aircraft; near term, airlines pass fuel costs through fares.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, CFO
quote: We are aligned with Boeing in terms of that, growing to that rate 31 in the second half of the year... On the 787... We ended the year in the, call it, low single-digit per month shipset rate... a good estimate would be about two per month as you think about the full year for 2022.
finding: RTX planned 2022 on Boeing reaching 737 rate 31 in H2 and 787 shipsets of only about 2 a month.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: Airbus, again, going from roughly 40 to, I think, about 48 or 49 a month by the end of the year... I know Airbus would like to take those rates up as high as they can as quickly as they can. But like everybody else, we're urging caution just because of the challenges of the supply chain.
finding: RTX openly urged Airbus to be cautious on A320 rate increases, pushing back on the airframer's ramp ambitions.
trigger: Airbus wants rates as high as possible, as fast as possible
response: urged caution because of supply-chain limits

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: I would tell you that we're in lockstep with both Airbus and Boeing on their production rates. Obviously, if you talk to the folks at Airbus, they'd like to see a rate of 70 or 75 by 2025. We'll see if we can get there, but we're certainly doing everything we can to support our customers there.
finding: RTX was noncommittal on Airbus's rate 70-75 ambition for 2025, promising support but doubting it would be reached.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: So I think, again, the airlines financially are doing very well. And the biggest concern they have is aircraft availability. And so we're going to see very strong inductions into the shop.
finding: RTX saw aircraft scarcity pushing airlines to keep older aircraft flying, which feeds engine shop visits.

doc: Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: At Airbus, I think they're at rate 48 today and rate 11, I think, on the A220... we think that Airbus by 2025 will be at rate 65. And Guil might say rate 75%, but we think rate 65 is doable.
finding: RTX judged only rate 65 by 2025 doable for the A320 family, below Airbus's rate-75 ambition, showing scepticism about airframer ramp plans.

doc: Morgan Stanley Laguna Conference (Company Conference Presentation)
speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: at Boeing, we think that by the end of the year, they will be in about 31 737s a month. We believe there will be about 2 787s a month... We think 737s will be back somewhere around 42 to 48 and 787 is back to probably 7 a month.
finding: RTX's planning view had Boeing recovering to 737 rate 42-48 and 787 rate about 7 by 2025.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO
quote: We expect strong growth on the commercial aerospace side to continue. RPMs will continue to recover back to the 2019 levels. And so we're going to see strong OE growth as Boeing and Airbus take up production rates. And we expect to see strong aftermarket growth as well
finding: RTX expected 2023 OE growth to be paced by Boeing and Airbus rate increases, with aftermarket growth from airlines adding capacity and keeping aircraft flying.

speaker: Christopher T. Calio, President & COO
quote: given the supply chain challenges we're having on perhaps new production, you're seeing airlines hold on to older assets longer, signing up for longer leases. So again, it kind of goes to the life of the V2500 maybe being some upside there.
finding: New-aircraft delivery shortfalls push airlines to keep older V2500 aircraft, which benefits P&W's legacy aftermarket.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO & Chairman
quote: We had some casting issues at Pratt & Whitney that was holding up delivery of engines to Airbus and other customers. That issue is still out there, although yields are getting better, processes are improving.
finding: P&W casting shortages held up engine deliveries to Airbus through 2022-23, making P&W a constraint on A320neo output.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO & Chairman
quote: On the Airbus side, I think last year, they were at 45 of the A320 family a month. Next year, they say they're going to 65. They didn't give a specific number on the -- for '23. But somewhere in that 50, mid-50 range, we'll be able to support that.
finding: P&W plans GTF output to Airbus's A320 ramp (45 to 65 a month) and says it can support mid-50s in 2023.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, CEO & Chairman
quote: In terms of 737 MAX, I think current production rate is about 31 a month. Boeing had talked about moving that up to 37 a month by the end of the year. ... But right now, again, I think Boeing has got some challenges.
finding: RTX tracks Boeing's 737 rate plans sceptically, noting Boeing's production challenges.

speaker: Christopher T. Calio, President & COO
quote: Customers understand what we're doing from a safety risk perspective and think we're doing the right thing, but they're certainly not happy with the net effect, and they've not been happy with the fleet health, even prior to powder metal and our output on MRO
finding: P&W acknowledges airline GTF customers were unhappy with fleet health and MRO output before the powder-metal issue.

speaker: Christopher T. Calio, President & COO (CEO-elect)
quote: Airbus, Boeing, what, 14,000 aircrafts in backlog today. Their positions are largely sold out through the decade. They've done a fantastic job driving demand for their product.
finding: RTX saw both airframers sold out through the decade, so near-term engine demand is set by production rates, not orders.

speaker: Neil G. Mitchill, EVP & CFO
quote: We've taken our rates down on the Boeing side in particular. But offsetting that or more than offsetting that is the aftermarket and the military side of Collins as well.
finding: RTX cut its Boeing production-rate assumptions mid-2024.

doc: Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna, Sep 2024)
speaker: Christopher T. Calio, CEO & President
quote: We are still like many in the industry calibrating with Boeing on what the rates are for '25 and beyond. Obviously, we've got a lot of capacity above and beyond what those rates are today.
finding: RTX's capacity exceeded Boeing's actual rates, so Boeing's production problems left it with idle capacity.

doc: Company Conference Presentation (Bernstein Strategic Decisions, May 2025)
speaker: Christopher T. Calio, Chairman & CEO
quote: When you think about NGSA though, I think for us, and we can debate when you think that ultimately sort of happens, there's varying sort of opinions on that. For purposes of this discussion, we'll just say maybe mid-next decade.
finding: P&W assumed Airbus's next single-aisle (NGSA) would come around the mid-2030s.

doc: Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna, Sep 2025)
speaker: Christopher T. Calio, Chairman & CEO
quote: Boeing has done obviously an excellent job continuing to ramp and build rate on 737, 787. I won't get into rates. That's for them to discuss, but I'll say that we're working exceptionally hard to make sure that we can flex to meet whatever they need
finding: By late 2025 RTX saw Boeing's 737 and 787 ramps as credible and was flexing capacity to follow them.

speaker: Bob Leduc, President of Pratt & Whitney
quote: When we get to the point where the mix at Pratt looks more like the mix at General Electric in terms of spares and OE, I am absolutely confident we're going to have industry-leading margins.
finding: Pratt sees GE's higher margins as the result of a spares-heavy mix from a large mature fleet, and expects to match them once its GTF fleet matures.

doc: Company Conference Presentation (Morgan Stanley Laguna, Sep 2016)
speaker: Greg Hayes, CEO
quote: Rolls recently announced they're going to move to our accounting next year. And they've certainly had some challenges associated with their own accounting, where they were deferring all of this margins over some 20 years and trying to recoup it over the aftermarket.
finding: UTC notes Rolls-Royce is abandoning its practice of deferring OE losses against 20 years of aftermarket, which had caused it problems.

quote: Customer selections of engines and components can also have a significant impact on later sales of parts and services. ... Pratt & Whitney’s major competitors in the sale of engines are GE Aviation, Honeywell, Turbomeca, and CFM International.
finding: P&W names GE Aviation and CFM as its main large-engine rivals and sees each engine selection as setting its later parts and services sales.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: If I take a look at some of the competitors in the engine business, it was a small stand-alone company without a big balance sheet, you've got some tougher headwinds out there in terms of financing, in terms of investments over the long term.
finding: UTC's CEO said stand-alone engine makers without large balance sheets face harder long-term financing of engine investments, a view of rivals' financial constraints.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: We have had discussions with them, as I think everybody else in the engine business has, in terms of a potential solution.
finding: P&W treated the Boeing NMA engine as an open competition in which all engine makers were in discussions with Boeing.

doc: Paris Air Show Investor Meeting (Special Call)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: When the V2500 was introduced, there was a 2-year period where we actually could not deliver V2500s because of the Rolls-Royce high compressor, 2 years. And I can remember that being the toughest 2 years in my career.
finding: P&W recalled that Rolls-Royce's high-pressure compressor in the IAE V2500 partnership caused a two-year delivery stoppage at entry into service, a precedent for partner-induced problems in engine joint ventures.

doc: Paris Air Show Investor Meeting (Special Call)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: today, 7,000 engines later, people will tell you that is among the best engine that powers the 320ceo. It's better in fuel burn than the CFM. It's as reliable.
finding: P&W claimed its V2500 beat the CFM56 on fuel burn and matched it on reliability on the A320ceo, using this to argue that early problems do not decide a programme's outcome.

quote: our aerospace businesses' competitors may offer substantial discounts and other financial incentives, performance and operating cost guarantees, and participation in financing arrangements, in an effort to compete for the aftermarket associated with these products. ... Pratt & Whitney’s major competitors in the sale of engines are GE Aviation, Honeywell, Safran Helicopter Engines, and CFM International.
finding: By 2017 UTC framed deep OE discounting and financing as something its competitors, including GE and CFM, do to win the aftermarket.

quote: Our aerospace businesses are subject to substantial competition from various domestic and foreign manufacturers, customers and companies that obtain regulatory agency approval to manufacture spare parts, with foreign companies sometimes receiving government research and development assistance, marketing subsidies and other assistance
finding: UTC sees foreign engine and aerospace rivals as benefiting from government R&D aid and subsidies, and PMA spare-parts makers as a competitive threat.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: As we designed the GTF, obviously, we designed it with maintenance cost in mind. Keep in mind, it's got 1,500 fewer airfoils than what you have on a V or what you have on a LEAP-X. So we have a pretty good handle, I would tell you, on what the cost should be on the FMPs.
finding: P&W claimed a structural maintenance-cost edge over CFM's LEAP (1,500 fewer airfoils) and used it to underwrite GTF fleet management plan pricing.

speaker: Gregory J. Hayes, Chairman & CEO
quote: every engine manufacturer, Rolls, GE, CFM, we've all said the same thing which is, we're interested in a sole-source opportunity there. We're not so interested in a dual source.
finding: According to P&W, Rolls-Royce also wanted sole source on the NMA and had little interest in a dual-source position.

doc: UTC 2019 Paris Air Show Investor and Analyst Meeting (incl. Raytheon/UTC CEO Q&A)
speaker: Robert F. Leduc, President, Pratt & Whitney
quote: we were disciplined on that campaign and we don't regret it. We think we made the right decision. And GE was known to be more aggressive than we were, and that's fine. But we are not worried about that.
finding: P&W says CFM/GE bid more aggressively on price to win IndiGo, and P&W chose discipline over matching.
response: Did not match GE's aggressive pricing

quote: Pratt & Whitney’s major competitors in the sale of engines are GE Aviation, Honeywell, Safran Helicopter Engines, and CFM International.
finding: In its FY2019 filing UTC named GE Aviation and CFM International (plus Honeywell and Safran Helicopter Engines) as P&W's major engine competitors and did not list Rolls-Royce. It saw the GE/CFM camp as its main rival.
